subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPRIMAND OF THOSE RESPONSIBLE FOR PROGRAM "CITIZEN McCAIN"-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On Tuesday, December 7, the CBC presented the regularly scheduled program "The Fifth Estate". Whereas this particular program, hosted by Adrianne Clarkson, entitled "Citizen McCain" gives unfavourable publicity to the major processing part of the agricultural industry of New Brunswick, it may have a detrimental effect on the marketing of agricultural products from the area and a resulting decrease in employment and in the general prosperity in the area; whereas the program by innuendo reflected upon the effectiveness of government programs of assistance to underdeveloped areas, and whereas the program was biased, inaccurate and totally improper, it will inevitably reflect upon the credibility of all CBC documentaries. Therefore, I move, under Standing Order 43, seconded by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan):
That the minister responsible for the CBC should, first, severely reprimand all those who were responsible for the preparation and presentation of this program; second, take the necessary steps to ensure that the CBC will never again present programs of such inaccuracy and bias; third, insist upon an apology to all those insulted by the demeaning program; and, fourth, have the officials responsible called before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts for their consideration.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a final supplementary question to the Minister of Finance? As it was a contention of the minister's two predecessors, Mr. Benson and Mr. Turner, that the revision of the tax system would not result in increased federal revenues over and above the amount they would have increased in the absence of the revision, and now that there has been a sensational increase in such revenues, would the minister inform the House of the government's intention regarding the $1.1 billion windfall which will accrue to the federal government if the revenue guarantee is cancelled?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: USE OF ALLEGED WINDFALL AS RESULT OF TERMINATION OF REVENUE GUARANTEE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman does not state the record correctly. The initial undertaking with regard to the revenue guarantee was with respect to the tax change, and a part of the amounts which have since become payable is, indeed, the consequence of the tax change. The substantial payments or liabilities which have accrued over the last four years have been payments made as a result of changes to the federal income tax law since tax reform and approved by this House. The provincial governments were advised, and that was one of the conditions in the agreement to which the parties came in 1971-72, that it was to be a five-year guarantee only, that it was to end in that period of time and that the provinces were to adjust to that change.
With regard to the so-called $900 million or $1 billion windfall, I remind hon. members that we have at the moment a federal deficit of $5 billion on a national accounts basis and it would be my wish to reduce that deficit. It would be my intention, as well.

subsubtopic: USE OF ALLEGED WINDFALL AS RESULT OF TERMINATION OF REVENUE GUARANTEE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Is that a commitment?

subsubtopic: USE OF ALLEGED WINDFALL AS RESULT OF TERMINATION OF REVENUE GUARANTEE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It would be my wish to reduce that deficit and I hope the hon. member opposite shares my concern for a reduced deficit. I should like to preserve for the federal government the freedom of action to engage perhaps in a tax reduction or other fiscal changes in the budget next time, and we can only preserve that by adhering to the revenue guarantee as originally contemplated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. A week ago today the Prime Minister said in the House, with reference to guidelines covering the behaviour of Crown corporations and practices in the hiring of overseas agents, as reported at page 1591 of Hansard:
Such guidelines do exist.. . they are contained in instructions and in draft model agreements which are circulated by certain ministers, those who have Crown corporations under their command.
This morning in the public accounts committee the chairman of AECL said with reference to those guidelines, in the case of the sale of a CANDU reactor to South Korea, that there were "no specifics whatsoever."

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: In other words, there was carte blanche.

speechtext: There were no specifics whatsoever in the appointment of Mr. Eisenberg, and that the practice of AECL was to hire a reputable agent and to "let him go to it." Can the Prime Minister explain the apparent contradiction between those two statements?

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not sure if it would be appropriate for me to comment on the proceedings of the committee as the hon. member has done in his question, but with your permission I will try to deal with the substance of the question. In my answer last week I indicated that guidelines existed and that they were applied by certain ministers to the corporations and agencies dependent on them. I did not say they existed in a uniform way for all areas, but I did say that it was the intention of the government to make a statement in the near future in which we will make an effort to have uniform guidelines applying across the whole board. The government would bring under one statement a series of practices which undoubtedly have been different over the years and not applied from time to time over the years and which have been somewhat different from department to department or Crown corporation to Crown corporation.

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister tell the House with what frequency the departments applied these guidelines? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the answer will be found in the substance of what will be put before the House very shortly. However, I find it important to remind the hon. member, and perhaps to tell him in advance, that there were practices within departments and indeed corporations which were spelled out in some detail. For the greater part, commercial practices which had been going on for many years in Canada and in other countries under this government and previous governments were just the normal rule of obeying the law and making sure you did not indulge in any fraudulent or corrupt practices.
Therefore, to the extent that this was the case there were no written guidelines covering every detail. It is assumed that Crown corporations and officials of the Canadian government operating in Canada or abroad know that they have to obey the law. There was no guideline required for that. However, in the intricate question of how-

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: Do they tell about judges?

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition has questions, but he never stands up to ask them.

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: As trading practices expanded in geography, size and intricacy, some departments found it useful to come up with models of contracts which should be adhered to. Others did not. It is in order to bring all this together that we will make a statement.

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext: Presumably the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Resources is one of the departments where we would have expected to have had in operation such guidelines. Therefore, will the Prime Minister inquire of the present Minister of Finance to find out from him why, when he was the minister responsible, he did not ensure that there were embedded into the agreement with Mr. Eisenberg certain specific guidelines as to how public money provided by the people of Canada was to be spent?

subsubtopic: ALLEGEDLY CONFLICTING STATEMENTS CONCERNING GUIDELINES ON USE OF AGENTS-REQUEST FOR TABLING GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I answered that question at least in part today and in previous days. We expect that the officials of Canada and the officials of Crown corporations will behave and conduct themselves according to law. This is a general position. Because of the fact that Crown corporations are at arms length, ministers do not run them on a day-to-day basis and the surveillance of government generally most fre-
Oral Questions
quently consists of looking at annual budgets and approving in a general way large expenditures. In many cases there was not a detailed examination of overseas arrangements. I repeat, the assumption was made by this government and by previous governments, including Tory governments and I am sure NDP governments in provincial areas, that officials would behave according to law. That was the practice and it is still the assumption.
I repeat, in very intricate dealings through agents in foreign countries, particularly in countries where the law of that country demands that a local agent be chosen, there were no detailed guidelines in existence for all departments and all Crown corporations. It is exactly that that we are proceeding to establish now.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR FAILURE TO BAN USE OF PESTICIDE LEPTOPHOS IN VIEW OF UNITED STATES ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Would the minister explain why, more than a year after the United States has banned the use of the organic pesticide leptophos, this dangerous chemical is still registered for use in Canada against insects on a variety of vegetable crops?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: REASON FOR FAILURE TO BAN USE OF PESTICIDE LEPTOPHOS IN VIEW OF UNITED STATES ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should explain how this product is used. It is used in the soil, not on crops, and we are satisfied that it cannot contaminate any harvested crops. It is also of interest to note that the chemical endrin has been banned for some time in Canada but the United States still uses it. We do know that there is a danger if this is used on fruits, vegetables, etc. We will not be using this product until next spring. It is used for cutworms etc., in the soil.
We are reviewing the situation with the other departments concerned, and perhaps if some of them will feel that it is the type of product that should be banned, it will be. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has already indicated that he will recommend that it be banned. 1 would point that if we have to go to some other kind of chemical to control pests in the soil, it will be much more costly to produce crops on that land.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Will the minister tell the House what efforts he has made to monitor the leptophos poisoning situation in the United States, what efforts he has made to monitor the use of this chemical in Canada; and in view of events south of the border, namely that it has been banned there, has the minister any plans to recommend discontinuation of this chemical in this country?

subsubtopic: CHANGES IN THE INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Is the government giving consideration to allowing a self-employed person who assists a spouse in a business to be able to file a separate income tax return and declare earnings and include such earnings for eligibility to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CHANGES IN THE INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Under our Canadian income tax system, the rates of income tax are progressive. That is, rates of tax increase on higher levels of income received by a taxpayer. Because of this progressivity, if a taxpayer were able to split his income with his spouse, he would avoid the increased rates of tax he would otherwise incur on higher levels of total income received by
80005-47y2

December 9, 1976
Order Paper Questions
him. Therefore, our income tax law does not recognize as income earned, amounts of remuneration paid by a taxpayer to his spouse for services performed in his unincorporated business. This long-standing feature of the tax law was debated in parliament at some length when the tax reform proposals were under consideration. It was not found possible to devise equitable rules to allow a payment of such wages as income to the spouse, without opening the way for many taxpayers to substantially reduce their tax by dividing their income for tax purposes with their spouses. This would be unfair to other taxpayers whose rates of tax increase as their incomes increase to higher levels. But where a corporation controlled by the taxpayer pays wages to his spouse, such wages are recognized as earnings of the spouse which she must declare as her own income (where the amount warrants it) and which entitles her to Canadian pension plan coverage. The use of a corporation for the business has two major effects. First, it establishes a third party which employs the wife. Secondly, corporations are required to meet many legislative standards which make it feasible to administer a test based upon whether the payments are reasonable remuneration for services performed. Moreover, where a taxpayer's spouse invests her own property to acquire a financial interest in his business or is actively engaged as a partner in the business, her share of the profits therefrom is also recognized for tax purposes, as her income which, similarly, qualifies her as eligible to make C.P.P. contributions. There is no immediate intention to change these well-established tax policies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that I and other hon. members of the House noted with particular interest your remarks immediately prior to our coming to this item of business when you indicated that later tonight we would be following the usual procedure and the House would be concurring in supplementary estimates and other expenditures of the government of Canada. I think that one of the major reasons we have chosen today to introduce this motion in the form we have is precisely that the usual procedure of the House of Commons, being simply to concur in, and not being able to call the government to account for its expenditures, has created a situation which has raised very severe questions about the competence of parliament to carry out its traditional role as a guardian of the public interest and as a controller of the public purse, which has been, in concert with other actions by this government-highlighted most recently by the report of the Auditor General-a further source of a decline in public confidence in the public institutions of Canada, a decline which should not affect us merely in our capacity as members of those particular institutions but also should concern us as it is an indication of a weakening of the ability of national institutions to earn the respect which alone can draw the country together.
December 9, 1976

I should say, in passing, that the respect for public institutions, particularly for parliament and for the conduct of governments, was not helped at all by suggestions which were made a couple of nights ago, and which have been repeated here by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), that somehow in this country it is unpatriotic for the provinces of Canada to adopt a common position which is a compromise position on all their parts in the face of a consistent tactic of the government opposite of attempting to divide the opinion of the provinces of Canada in federal-provincial relations and trying to triumph by a tactic of divide and conquer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Blackmail; that's what it is.

For some time now, Mr. Speaker, Canadians have been more and more concerned and asking questions about the value and merits of their national institutions. Unfortunately we must admit that they are right to ask those questions. Their very existence depends on respect from the people. It is the duty of the government and of Parliament to earn for them the respect of Canadians. Flowever the attitude of the present government is about to jeopardize the credibility of our national institutions.
I think, sir, that we have all been concerned with the practice that has become evident again today in questions relating to the public nature of the federal-provincial discussions which will occur next week and those which occurred earlier this week. We in Canada now face a situation where to an increasing degree decisions of fundamental importance to the future of the country are taken by small groups of people who theoretically are responsible, but who in practice are meeting in secret to make decisions in secret which are relayed back to the respective legislatures, whether the parliament of Canada or the legislatures of particular provinces, for ratification.
That has rather seriously changed the system of government we have had in this country. It raises serious questions about how the parliamentary system functions and the way the system was established, namely, to allow members elected from the various constituencies of the land to control in a real sense the actions of the executive of the day. Parliament must begin with information, and it must involve influence. If the parliament of Canada continues to be denied information and influence on the activities of the government of Canada, we have strayed a serious distance from the original purposes of the parliamentary system.
Today the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised a very legitimate question when he asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) by what authority, in terms of the long history of parliament, the decisions of import to the country-those that were under discussion earlier this week and will be again next week-should be made, in effect, in secret by a group of people who, while theoretically respon-
Economic Policy
sible, have the capacity to impose their private decisions on the various legislatures of the land. The Prime Minister, who is probably the expert in the House of Commons on strawmen, dismissed this very valid request by the hon. member for Edmonton West as setting up a strawman. It is not that at all; it is a question of real concern to all of us who want to see the parliamentary system in Canada function and represent the people of Canada.
Unfortunately, the practice of secrecy which the Prime Minister, at least, is not prepared to initiate breaking down in relation to the federal-provincial conference next week has become a practice very close to the heart of this government. As my colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has pointed out on numerous occasions, this is a government almost obsessive in its secrecy. We have seen it refuse, not simply to make information available to people who should be informed both by formal right and informal right, but we have also seen it frequently make decisions which suffer because they are based on the narrow range of information.
We have seen this most recently in the Speech from the Throne which began this session of parliament. The government proposed to begin consultations on the anti-inflation process-some 13 months after the process was brought into being-not to try to draw upon the advice of Canadians and the advice of interested sectors of the country but, instead, to try to get some help in bailing the government out of a situation it got into by acting too much in contempt of the advice that could and should have been offered by various interested parties in the country.
The federal government apparatus has quite aptly been called by the Auditor General-and, I believe, by the Prime Minister-"the largest business in Canada." In terms of its spending impact, it is equivalent to the 20 largest corporations in Canada. Yet we have here, in this massive instrument of impact upon the conduct of Canadian affairs, a complete absence of direction, an absence of leadership, an absence of purpose. In the face of that situation, this largest business in the country has become, in effect, an uncontrolled political conglomerate which, unfortunately, in its lack of purpose and lack of direction is setting a trend for other levels of government and a trend of carelessness for the public purse.
We believe that it is fundamental to restore fiscal control to the House of Commons and the government of Canada. We think that unless there is a demonstration on the part of the government that it is concerned about fiscal control, unless there is a demonstration that the parliament of Canada has a capacity to control the spending practices of the government of Canada, we are going to continue to invite the cynicism which is unfortunately undermining the respect for institutions in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that if that cynicism persists it is going to have serious effects, not simply on the Financial capacities and on the economic policy of the govern-

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy
ment of Canada, but it is going to have a serious and deteriorating effect upon the capacity of this institution of parliament and the institution of the government of Canada to command respect and draw together Canadians in achieving our other goals, whether they be in terms of social policy, national unity or anything else.
When the Auditor General introduced his report, the attention of many of us was initially drawn to what one of the newspapers called the "horror" stories. We are aware of many of these horror stories and the failure to make optimum use or anything near optimum use of office space, transfer expenses not accounted for, inadequate control of cash received in many departments, expenditures seriously in excess of appropriations that are approved-we know about the individual horror stories. We have to recognize that the reports of Auditors General, particularly the most recent one but also those which preceded it, have to be seen not as a mere catalogue of mistakes but, instead, as a thorough indictment of the system of control that has been in place in the government of Canada for the last eight years.
The recommendation of the Auditor General that a chief financial officer be appointed in each department seems to be under way, if we can judge from the responses given in this House by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) yesterday to questions the origin of which might be a matter of dispute.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: They change their minds from day to day.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: As my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) points out, they change their minds from day to day; but the problem with the House of Commons is that we still do not know exactly what kind of system the President of the Treasury Board intends to bring in.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: He does not, either.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: We do not know if he intends to bring in any system at all. If a chief financial officer is to be brought into each department of government, the House of Commons would like to know from the minister-and if he participates in the debate later, perhaps he will tell us-at what level these officers will be appointed in the departments. There is a very real danger, if they are named at a level too subordinate to the deputy minister, that they are going to be unable to exercise the kind of control that is important. If they are not able to do that, then their appointments will be phantom and their authority will be nil. We would like to know from the minister at precisely what level these officers will be appointed, and precisely what their functions and powers will be.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: And whose idea it was.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn), of course-a naturally modest man-is interested in having on the record precisely whose idea it was. Even if there is an introduction of this kind of representation, it is clear that it is only part of the step that must be taken by the
(Mr. Clark ]
government to repair a situation where its expenditures are, in the words of the Auditor General, "virtually out of control".
In addition, even if we are able to make the kinds of reforms proposed by the Auditor General of Canada, it is clear that there is going to be one part of, or one half of, a necessary two-pronged effort to restore fiscal control to the federal government of Canada. It will help only to give direction and control in a bureaucratic sense; it will not, by itself, serve to restore public confidence.
The present runaway situation in public finance is associated with two developments. The first development has been the partial-I emphasize "partial"-implementation of the recommendations of the Glassco royal commission for decentralization of fiscal control. There has been a decentralization of authority without the mechanisms for control and responsibility. The other matter which is of critical importance is that there has also been, in the period since 1965, a gradual and striking removal from the House of Commons of any effective capacity to control the spending or planning of the government of Canada.
In passing, it is important to dwell for a moment on the degree to which the reforms proposed by the Glassco commission have only been partially introduced. I will accept, as I am sure the House will, the authority of the Auditor General of Canada himself when he says:
However, it seems clear that the present unsatisfactory and vulnerable situation came about because certain key recommendations on financial management and control made by the Royal Commission on Government Organization (Glassco commission) in 1962 were not implemented. Perhaps they were not understood, although the recommendations relating to the decentralization of financial authorities were evidently understood and were fully implemented.
The Auditor General goes on to say:
Unfortunately, the concurrent and equally important Glassco recommendation that new counterbalancing controls be instituted and that existing ones be strengthened was not implemented.
Sir, I now want to turn the attention of the House to the problems faced by this parliament in dealing with the public spending of the government and the problems faced by parliament in exercising the traditional parliamentary role of controlling, in the final analysis, government expenditure and government plans. I will not dwell long on what we can call the former situation. It is clear to all who have studied parliament and know of its force that there was a time, not long ago, when the House of Commons had a real capacity to call the government of Canada to account. It was not simply a matter of giving, as we shall be called upon tonight to give, automatic passage to expenditure requirements-not at all. There was, with the capacity for unrestricted questioning of estimates, the real ability to force the government to respond to the will of the public of Canada.
One authority upon whom I shall call is Professor Norman Ward, author of the book entitled "The Public Purse." He referred to that historic event in Canadian parliamentary history which has become known as the pipeline debate, when the opposition of that day was able to use its capacity to delay
December 9, 1976

passage of the estimates to force the government of Canada into a difficult situation. I quote Professor Ward, who said:
No one who witnessed that sitting of the House could have any doubts of the power of the weapon which the members held until spokesmen for the various opposition parties made clear that they had chosen to lay it down.
No observer of any of the processes which will occur later this evening in this House can have any doubt that the parliament of Canada has lost completely that capacity to control expenditures and approve the plans of a majority government in Canada today. There was, with that former system, an obvious shortcoming: it took too long. As government has become more complex, it is no longer possible to have the unrestrained capacity on the part of the opposition to hold up public business. Everyone recognizes that we could not contemplate, with the modern agenda of business, the kinds of delays which were possible perhaps in easier times. The difficulty is, sir, that the reforms which were introduced, particularly the way they have been interpreted by the government opposite, have substituted for delay a much more serious problem in that they have left the parliament of Canada virtually without control of the public spending of Canada, and virtually without control of the government of Canada, it is significant to note that when there were changes in methods of financial control, there were, by coincidence, at the same time changes in the rules of the House of Commons.
To be consistent on the matter of questioning the estimates, it would be helpful to the House of Commons to review some of the changes which have occurred in the last few years in the handling of estimates by this government and the presentation of estimates by this government to the House of Commons. One change was that detailed information was dropped from estimates and millions of dollars were put under headings which gave little information. For example, the preface to one set of estimates says that they are to assist members of parliament in their deliberations and to assist those seeking an understanding of the purposes for which the government proposes funds to be appropriated.
In 1970-71, the form of the estimates was changed with that particular goal in mind. In fact what has happened, as all know who have served on committees trying to scrutinize estimates, is that a sentence or two is placed in front of items allocating funds-a sentence or two which can be highly uninformative. For example, some in this House have recently been preoccupied with the discontinuance of the ferry service in British Columbia. I happen to have obtained a copy of the 1976-77 estimates for the Department of Transport, and I note that ferry services are defined in the following detail:
Development, implementation and monitoring of programs, including participation in policy formulation, for the operation of certain coastal, ferry and related terminal services, particularly those for which Canada has accepted responsibility under terms of union and confederation.
That explanation gave next to no detail, but that item cost in excess of $116 million. On the basis of a handful of words, the parliament of Canada is now supposed to pass intelligent judgment and to raise questions upon expenditure in excess of $116 million. I have cited an example which was simply drawn at random, because it is of some concern now; but it indicates
Economic Policy
the kinds of changes which have taken place in the period since 1971-72. It indicates a moving away by the government, in its presentation of estimates to parliament, from the giving of detailed information with regard to estimates, and this moving away generally makes it very difficult for the parliament of Canada to do its job.
The other highly serious problem which we face as a parliament now, and which the people of Canada face as a consequence, is that the committees of parliament, and parliament itself, have been deprived of any leverage upon the government by the automatic guillotine which comes into force to conclude debate. The government has the capacity in the committees, through its control of committee chairmen-a control which exists in reality, as any realist in this House must admit-to decide who is going to testify and for how long. That is done through the steering committees. They have also the capacity to formally limit debate.
Last year, as an experiment, some estimates were brought before the House, presumably for debate along the old lines. The problem was that debate was under the guillotine; it was to end that very night. Consequently, any minister under questioning knew that he had simply to turn up his collar against the storm; he knew he had only to live through that day. Indeed, he encouraged-and I say this with respect to the sensitivity of the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin)-supporters of the government party to consume as much time as they could by asking patsy questions. That was allowable perhaps within the rules, but it was a shameful use of those rules and shameful contempt of the right of parliament to control expenditure.

speechtext: Do you people live in glass houses?

speechtext:
Theoretically, this House of Commons retains the ability to vote down estimates, although this very rarely happened in the past even before the rules changed. It has not happened at all since 1970-71, not even in a minority parliament. It was not possible for the House of Commons to ratify, in the whole House, changes which had been made in the various standing committees.
In June, 1973, I remember a number of committees reporting back to the House of Commons recommending specific expenditure cuts. I particularly remember being involved in one which recommended the reduction by $1 million of consultants' expenditures for the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. That expenditure was struck out in committee. However, the government brought it back in in a form, not where it would be considered as a $1 million expenditure struck out for the reasons decided by the majority of the Standing Committee of the House of Commons, but part of an over-all estimate of $45 million. It was included with a number of other quite legitimate expenditures, expenditures which the committee was quite prepared to accept.
With that kind of juggling and varying of an expenditure to which exception was taken in a body of expenditures that we
80005-48i/2

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy
were prepared to accept, the government was in a position of, in effect, blackmailing the House of Commons into supporting an expenditure which it did not want to support. That kind of trickery and deceit has an opportunity to occur only with a minority government. The point I am making is that there is a determination on the part of this government to use the changes that have occurred in the method of bringing forward the estimates to frustrate the will of parliament even though that will is expressed by standing committees of the House.
I want to review very quickly a couple of other problems which exist in the present system of consideration of estimates in committee. One obvious problem is that there is very little public attention paid to the activities of standing committees, particularly when considering estimates. Second, there is a clear inability for members of parliament of any party who are interested in getting at the facts about a particular expenditure effectively to cross-examine a chairman or minister who is determined to stop that kind of cross-examination. By controlling the agenda, or having limited time, the government can effectively forestall any kind of investigation. There is, by the nature of reference, a simple inability on the part of the House of Commons to deal with a specific matter in any prolonged or coherent fashion.
I see that the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury) is in the chamber. In the last session, that distinguished member was a member of the government of Canada. We had an admission by that gentleman, as a minister, that the government of Canada was indulging in the practice of hiding certain expenditures, particularly those that related to intelligence activities by the government of Canada. That raises the very serious problem about the ability of parliament to control the expenditures of government. We have no capacity to know what amounts of money are being spent on intelligence operations, or for any other purpose, by the government of Canada.
I should say that there was an undertaking, although I do not believe it has been acted on, to give private briefings to members of parliament who were interested in that question.
The far more serious problem was that the then minister admitted there had been an inflation of other estimates by smuggling in the intelligence estimates. We do not know in how many other cases this occurred. However, it is clear that the parliament of Canada was being deliberately misled as to the amount of money the government of Canada intended to spend on particular projects. The government intended to deflect part of that sum to intelligence activities which it did not trust parliament to know about. That is another indication of the abuse of the system in which the present government has indulged.
This is not an academic matter. Today we face another very real concern about the capacity of parliament and parliamentary committees to investigate. I am told by my colleagues who serve on the public accounts committee that many of the documents necessary for that fundamentally important committee of parliament to examine the records of AECL may be withheld for a variety of spurious reasons.

I appreciate that courtesy, Mr. Speaker, and I will attempt to be brief. Consideration should be given to vest in the committees of the House of Commons some capacity to initiate investigations into matters of public interest. Right now, the capacity of committees is limited. Their capacity to investigate is limited in two ways. First, we know from experience that estimates before a committee is an inadequate means of examining the government. The second would be to receive a reference from the House, in theory, but from the government in fact. The practice is that when the subject is hot, the reference does not come. Time and time again, this parliament has sought to have the committees of the parliament of Canada empowered to look into questions of obvious public importance. Time after time the government has refused to make that kind of reference.
We think it very much worth considering having some capacity vested in the committees of the House of Commons to
December 9, 1976

initiate their own inquiries. They would be both extensive and educational. If we are looking for parliamentary reform, we might consider looking, not to another country but simply to the other place. It is one of the ironies of political life in this country that private members of the other place have far more capacity to look into public problems than private members of the House of Commons.
1 want, in passing, to pay tribute to the members of the other place in recognition of some of the very important investigations they have carried out, performing the kind of function which the elected parliament of Canada should perform. I think it is unacceptable that the appointed members of a national institution should have more power and capacity to investigate than do the elected members.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: There are number of other matters to which I wished to refer, Mr. Speaker, but I will abbreviate those references. 1 do wish to say, however, that one of the other constraints upon the capacity of parliament to secure information has been the change in attitude of the government toward the question period. We all recognize that there is no requirement upon the government to answer questions put to it in the House of Commons. But there is a requirement on the part of the government of Canada to treat seriously questions which are posed seriously in the House. Unfortunately, we have seen the development of what I think can fairly be characterized as a personal style of flippant answers, being cute with questions, of seeking not to answer, not to provide information but, rather, to evade questions and create false controversies and to send people off on tangents. We get responses, rather than answers, from ministers opposite, and I think if there were a serious desire on the part of ministers to inform the House of Commons they could start by answering seriously questions seriously posed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: This motion, among other things, condemns the government for its inept handling of the public finances of Canada. Its record in the handling of public finances is well known. When the present administration took office, federal expenditures were in the neighbourhood of $9 billion a year. Today they exceed $42 billion. When the government took office, governments in Canada claimed 30 per cent of the gross national product. Today they claim almost 43 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That's all government in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That is right. The parliamentary secretary makes an interjection which is correct. But he would not want to pretend that the initiative for that increase came exclusively or even primarily from other levels of government. In the last decade in particular-and this is documentable-that initiative came from the federal government. It has been the central
Economic Policy
cause of the increase in the growth of public sector consumption of the gross national product in this country.
Despite all the increase in expenditures, we have so little to show in terms of public response. Rather than an increased faith in the government's ability to help Canadians meet their difficulties, there is now an increasing growth of cynicism and a diminution of trust about the role and relevance of government policies to the economic well-being of Canada. Rather than a major increase in our well-being as a nation, we see our country has slipped in one decade from second place to seventh place in the world in terms of per capita living standards. It threatens to fall even farther down the list. Instead of there being greater sense of economic equality in Canada, we see instead a greater sense of division among the regions and among the different income groups.
I do not wish to take the time of the House to elaborate on economic details about which my colleagues will be speaking later on in the debate. But there are a least two aspects of the present situation which are fundamental. The first is something I have enunciated on many occasions when speaking across the country. It is the need for us to halt, and gradually reverse, the growing claims of all governments upon our national output. I am convinced that what is often referred to as "the British disease" is a very real economic malady. I have no reason to believe that if we continue to hurtle down the course set by the government we will avoid our own particular Canadian strain of that disease. Indeed, we will invite it. I want to make it clear that my colleagues in the Conservative party and I are advocating a far different approach to spending restraint than that which is practised by the government. The government opposite bows in the direction of restraint, although the minister admitted the other day that in fiscal year 1977 federal government expenditures will increase by 14 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Fourteen per cent this year, and only 11 per cent next year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: The minister tells me 14 per cent this year, and 11 per cent next year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Dreadful.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: We find it interesting that the saving will be in the neighbourhood of $1.2 billion. It is both interesting and illustrative that that is exactly the figure the government of Canada, in the negotiations between finance ministers which failed this week in Ottawa, is seeking to take from the provinces of Canada. So the government practises restraint, not by restraining its own expenditures but by passing its burdens on to other levels of government. That is not restraint; that is sleight-of-hand.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, Hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Clearly, what we need to do is not to pass the buck on to the provinces but, instead, exercise national leadership to try to bring together the efforts at restraint to all levels of government.

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy

There is another major difference between our approach and theirs, that is, the relation between the federal spending policy and that of the other levels of government. One of the favorite tackles of this government in limiting its expenditures is quite senselessly to shift its commitments on the provinces, and to hell with the taxpayers: they have no choice but to support all governments.
In our approach, we endeavour to generate a coordinated and joint effort on the part of all levels of government with a view to moderating the overall demand on the economy. I underestimate neither the difficulty nor the complexity of that endeavour, but it is necessary: otherwise, we will witness no less than the abdication of the leadership.
This brings me to the second point I want to stress in this context. It is obvious for everybody, except the government, that we cannot continue making decisions which affect more than two fifths of our national economy on the basis of the arbitrary and unilateral action of eleven different governments. And yet that is what we do in Canada. The federal and provincial governments make their budgetary decisions separately, without real co-ordination, which often puts them in competition, if not in opposition.

Of course, the ministers of finance meet, as they did earlier this week. But I do not think any of us would pretend, in the present atmosphere, that they even seek to achieve any meaningful co-ordination of the economic direction of what amounts to two fifths of our national output. This, clearly, is not a one-sided affair. The fault-if that is the term I should use-does not rest solely with the federal government. The government has contributed-significantly to the whole problem of governments acting unilaterally in a country requiring co-operation, but it is not the exclusive agent of that kind of action.
It is fair to assert, however, that only the federal government can show the kind of national leadership we need if we are to achieve worth-while economic co-ordination within the public sector. Along with maintaining security, the management of the national economy is probably the most fundamental responsibility of the federal government. It controls the monetary system, and while it does not by any means exercise all the fiscal power, it controls the national fiscal lever and thus, in a very real way, sets the framework for everyone else. Only the national government can exercise the primary responsibility for economic management in Canada.
In the name of that responsibility there must be a much greater effort, a much more concerted active national leadership in seeking to co-ordinate, through consensus and through compromise, the impact of public sector policies and demands upon our economy as a whole. That will mean, not a giving up of ultimate responsibility by the government of Canada but a greater willingness on the part of all governments to act as partners and to share information and planning before each exercises the responsibility which ultimately rests with each.
| Mr. Clark.)
I began, Mr. Speaker, by speaking about the problems that face our national institutions, such as the erosion of respect which can have consequences of very real danger to a country like ours. This parliament is the only institution in Canada which legitimately speaks for all the people of Canada. It is our only national institution. But it can have effect only if it has power. It can be respected by the people of Canada only if it is respected by the government of Canada. The tragic situation today is that the government of Canada has demonstrated, through its use of changed rules, through its failure to bring forward estimates which can be understood, through its refusal to accept the control or the point of view of the House of Commons, what amounts to contempt for parliament which, unfortunately, is capable of being shared by the people of Canada. We believe that that kind of attitude by the government must be changed. We would hope that in the acceptance of the motion introduced today we will be beginning down the road toward a change in that fundamental attitude.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with considerable interest to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who read the motion that has triggered this debate. I must say I find it rather interesting, and passing strange, that the motion comes barely one week after the Prime Minister of Australia, the Right Hon. Malcolm Fraser, announced the decision of his government to proceed with a fundamental reorganization of the central management functions of the government of Australia along the lines of what the Australians call "the Ottawa model".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
This reorganization was announced after careful consideration by Mr, Fraser's cabinet of the recommendations of the royal commission on Australian government administration; and of all the management systems examined by this commission-and indeed there were several and many-the system that we have gradually been implanting in the federal government of Canada was found to be the most effective. Allow me to quote from the statement issued on November 30, by the treasurer of Australia, the Hon. Phillip Winch:
The division of existing Treasury functions is along the lines of the "Ottawa model" that has produced excellent results in Canada . . .
The new arrangements reflect the Commonwealth's desire to generally upgrade and improve the working efficiency of the public service . . . They are
December 9, 1976

evidence of the government's determination to strengthen its sources of economic advice and to exercise more effective control over expenditures.
A bit of a coincidence, Mr. Speaker! Barely a week after the government of Australia, a fellow member of the Commonwealth and one of the world's major liberal democracies, decided to adopt "the Ottawa model" of financial administration, the leader of our Conservative opposition has seen fit to make a blanket condemnation of the government for its handling of the public funds of Canada. He and his colleagues have been doing so throughout the course of the last few days by misquoting and misrepresenting with almost total abandon a considerable and substantial report by the Auditor General of Canada.
This government welcomes the special audits, the publication of special studies and the inquiries undertaken in the last fiscal year by the distinguished gentleman who holds the office of auditor general. Not only in the exercise of our responsibilities do we welcome those studies and the recommendations accompanying them, but it is the fact that it is the government that has made this possible, co-operating fully with the Auditor General and increasing considerably in recent years the financial and human resources allocated to his office.
At the end of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like, with the permission of the House, to take the opportunity of tabling a summary of the Auditor General's estimates during the past five years. Since the appointment of the present incumbent, the financial resources allocated to that office have gone from $4.4 million annually to $13.9 million, an increase of about 215 per cent over a four-year period. The man-years authorized for that office have risen from 298 persons to 428 over the same period, an increase of more than 43 per cent. In other words, the Auditor General's office has been one of the fastest growing, most strongly supported functions of parliament, supported by the federal government.
In effect, the Auditor General has requested of us that his office be exempted from the expenditure restraint program introduced by the government a year ago, and Treasury Board had approved this request. We have done so because Treasury Board ministers were very conscious of the crucial role that the Auditor General plays in the intricate system of checks and balances through which Canadians seek to ensure that public funds are used and handled efficiently and effectively and, most importantly, in accordance with the statutory provisions set by parliament.
We are also fully aware of the very important contribution that the Auditor General, through an expansion of his activities into what could be called system audits, can make toward the improvement of financial management and control systems in the public service of Canada. As a result, the estimates for his office have been increased by about 58 per cent in the current fiscal year, from $8.8 million to almost $14 million, inclusive of the $2 million tabled a few days ago in Supplementary Estimates (B). That is more than four times as much as the increase of about 14 per cent this year in the over-all expenditures of the government.
Economic Policy
Similarly, the authorized man-years of the Auditor General's office have been increased by 7 per cent this year, more than 41/2 times the percentage increase effected through the whole of the public service of Canada. I want to inform the House once again that we willingly acquiesce in the request of the Auditor General that his office be exempted from expenditure restraints for the year 1977-78.
I am also pleased to remind this House that the proposed legislation which I tabled on November I has been drafted after very close consultation with the Auditor General. I refer to the Auditor General's Act. We have done this out of the glare of attention and political controversy, and 1 think it has been extremely successful. 1 think, too, that hon. members will find that, with the exception of minor points which he has informed me about and may wish to raise at the committee stage, the provisions of Bill C-20, which is the Auditor General's Act, have received the unqualified endorsement of the Auditor General.
On August 26 he reported to the deputy secretary for financial administration of the Treasury Board that his advisers, Mr. Belanger, Mr. Campbell, Mr. Skinner and Mr. Dunnet, were unanimous in the opinion that the draft legislation meets the spirit of the independent review committee's report and implements most of its recommendations, and that he agreed fully with their views. He said that he saw no need, in the face of this, for further discussion of the provisions of the draft act, because he expresses the view that it captures well the essence of the Wilson committee reports, and in his opinion it was ready for submission to parliament. He thanked the deputy secretary for his very active participation in bringing that extremely important legislation to fruition, or to its present stage.
I think that is a reasonable rebuttal to the misinformed, misleading and often partisan view expressed in this House and in the press in the past weeks of the government's record concerning financial administration, and in complete disregard of the many initiatives detailed in the progress report I tabled in the House on November 19, about which 1 am sure the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) is going to have something to say. In light of these facts it was, therefore, in a somewhat different perspective that I saw the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year 1975-76. 1 did not stop at the first five sections of the report. I read through the special audits and inquiries reported in the other eight sections and focused on the audit operations and specific observations contained in the subsequent six sections. I want to make it absolutely clear that each of these special audits, inquiries and specific observations contained therein is being carefully reviewed by the Treasury Board and each department or agency concerned or involved, and I also assure the House that remedial action will be taken and, as in previous years, will be reported thoroughly to the public accounts committee.
I also want to make the point that most of the observations made by the Auditor General, following the special audits and

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy
inquiries which he conducted in this past fiscal year, confirm the Treasury Board's own views, its own findings, as well as the timeliness of initiatives we have taken to correct these deficiencies. I am referring, for example, to the Auditor General's comments about management and control systems for office accommodation, for travel and relocation expenses, and payrolls, to which the hon. Leader of the Opposition made reference in his comments at the opening of this debate.
I want to emphasize that our initiatives have not been limited to those undertaken by the financial administration branch of the secretariat, about which I also reported to the House on November 19. Members should be aware that on March 25, eight months ago, my predecessor announced the appointment of a senior committee on administration improvements to make recommendations to Treasury Board and to cabinet on required changes in the public service management system and on the most effective ways of implementing and monitoring those changes.
Among the key areas examined by that committee-which, incidentally, is chaired by the secretary of the Treasury Board and composed of the clerk of the Privy Council and the deputy ministers of nine departments-were office accommodation and travel regulations, and I will soon be reporting to the House on the work done by that committee on changes to regulations, procedures and practices which it has recommended to the Treasury Board and which we will be implementing forthwith.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, a personnel policy branch of the secretariat has been developing a new and improved government-wide pay system, a subject of some concern, in close co-operation with the Department of Supply and Services, as well as with the financial administration branch which is concurrently developing financial control standards for payroll systems.
Referring to the more specific audit observations made by the Auditor General, I should like to point out that those made in sections 14, 15 and 16 of his annual report deal with the presentation of government accounts and that most of the discrepancies, with generally accepted accounting practices noted by the Auditor General, had already been recognized in the study of the accounts of Canada initiated by the government in 1974 and sponsored by the Treasury Board secretariat and, indeed, referred to the public accounts committee last year.
Members are, or should be, aware that amendments to the Financial Administration Act are required to correct these discrepancies, and I assure hon. members that these amendments will be introduced by the government early in the new year. Among those is the amendment that will clearly establish the Treasury Board as the single central agency, which the Treasury Board thinks it should be and which the Auditor General also has recommended as necessary action.
Of the 22 specific audit observations made in sections 17 and 18 of the report, 11 were accounting improprieties which did not actually involve any loss to Canadian taxpayers. For example, a quite legitimate payment to the province of

Manitoba was improperly charged to the appropriations for 1975-76 instead of those for 1976-77. Several other accounting improprieties are of this nature. They do reflect the inadequacy of present fiscal year-end procedures. In fact, as I announced in the progress report I tabled on November 19, these procedures will be changed shortly through appropriate amendments to the Financial Administration Act, following completion of the required studies by the financial administration branch of the Treasury Board secretariat.
Other specific audit observations did involve the probable loss of public moneys. The Auditor General reported, for example, that we failed to recover costs of trans-border highway services between Canada and the United States; that we were paying rent on property not occupied; that we were getting too low a return on long-term mortgage credits to farmers; that the guidelines for determining ferry deficits were inadequate; that we had purchased and modified a vessel unfit for navigation, and so on. Those are the so-called horror stories which have been so prominently displayed in the press out of the millions of transactions completed by federal departments and agencies last year. Out of all of them there were 11 such horror stories reported by the Auditor General.
It is difficult, admittedly, to estimate what the actual losses to taxpayers have been, because in most cases some recovery of the funds is possible and will, indeed, be attempted. I have asked my officials to try to put a valuation on the total maximum possible loss arising from these improprieties, and again, I emphasize, in the absence of any recovery. The total amount computed is about $6.6 million, of which only $85,000 consists of losses incurred through fraud, default or mistakes of any persons-in effect, what are technically called defalcations.
The $6.5 million is a considerable amount of money, and the deficiencies noted by the Auditor General which have caused these potential losses will be promptly reviewed and remedied by the Treasury Board, as they have been in past years. It must be remembered that the total dollar value of transactions conducted by the government of Canada in the fiscal year 1975-76 was over $129 billion. We expended about $34 billion under budgetary appropriation. Non-budgetary receipts amounted to another $32 billion. Our non-budgetary outlays amounted to $33 billion, yet the maximum value of losses discovered by the Auditor General, provided we do not recover any of it, represent .00005 per cent, or one-twenty thousandths of all the moneys transacted during the fiscal year by all federal departments and by all federal agencies.
Let us keep this in perspective, although I am extremely concerned that we improve our fiscal management and our financial control mechanisms. There is no doubt that, as the Auditor General has pointed out, some federal practices in financial administration are unacceptable-and we are determined to eliminate these practices. But setting aside any extravagant statements that may appear in the House or in the press, it is my contention that parliament and the government
December 9, 1976

are very much in control of the public purse and that they exercise this control through time-tested and effective institutions, systems and procedures.
What do we mean when we speak of the public purse? First, we are speaking of the close to $38 billion in revenues which will be collected during the current fiscal year by Revenue Canada and other federal agencies. Can anyone seriously argue that we have lost control of our taxation system? Deductions at source are regularly remitted to the Receiver General of Canada. Taxation Canada is better equipped than ever before to handle the millions of income tax returns which will be filed in the first few months of 1977, and we expect assessment notices and reimbursements, where justified, to be swiftly dispatched to taxpayers. Indeed, Canadian taxpayers can testify, sometimes rather ruefully, that government control over tax revenues is only too thorough.
Can anyone seriously claim that the government, or indeed parliament, has lost or is close to losing control over social security payments? Each months millions of cheques are being issued to and received by Canadians: old age pensions, family allowances, unemployment insurance payments, veterans pensions, Manpower training allowances-more than $9 billion worth in the current fiscal year and about 22 per cent of total federal expenditures. I emphasize that all these payments are made by government departments and agencies in accordance with the statutory provisions set by parliament.
Can anyone seriously claim that parliament or the cabinet has lost control of payments to other governments? In the current fiscal year, over $8 billion-close to one-fifth of our total expenditures-will be remitted to provincial governments and municipal or territorial administrations. All of these payments are being made under formulas stipulated in statutes of this parliament which were adopted, in the main, after lengthy discussions in the democratic parliamentary process. I am referring to fiscal transfer payments, hospitalization payments, medicare payments, contracting-out payments, post-secondary education payments, and so on. Some of the acts governing these payments will shortly be up for renewal. Ministers have stated in the House and in other places the views and intentions of the government with regard to the methods of their reintroduction, and opposition members will have ample opportunity to state their views and counterviews on this matter in the House and in its committees.
I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker. Holders of government bonds can testify that the public debt is efficiently managed and they get the interest due to them when it is due. These interest charges will amount this year to about $5 billion, another 10 per cent of our total expenditures. Recipients of oil compensation payments or subsidies for transportation, agriculture and fishing can similarly testify to the efficiency of our expenditure management systems. Opposition members of the House can themselves vouch for the effectiveness of parliamentary control over this category of expenditure since just the other day they succeeded in persuading the government to accept their amendment to the government expenditure restraint bill.

You are also aware, Mr. Speaker, that the standing committees of the House-and I want to refer to the comments of the Leader of the Opposition on how the House cannot deal with estimates-devote more than 500 hours each year to detailed examination of the estimates submitted by the government under the processes approved by this parliament. Our Standing Orders provide for 25 allotted days during which opposition parties can initiate debate on any aspects of the government's record including, of course, expenditures. Questions placed on the order paper, as well those put in the oral question period, allow members of the House to query ministers each day on every aspect of their activities, including the expenditure of funds.
Month after month the remainder of our sitting days are devoted to the detailed examination in the House or in standing committees or ad hoc committees of every piece of legislation introduced by the government. Practically every one of them involves expenditures in one way or another. So if hon. members are not exercising effective control of the public purse through that manner, I am very puzzled at what the devil we are doing here every day.
I can only conclude that the real problem we are facing- one which is serious and which concerns us very much-is not really that parliament or the government have lost control of the public purse, but that some of our processes and procedures, bookkeeping systems and practices are inadequate and that this has understandably given rise to uncertainty about the efficiency and, indeed, the propriety of government operations.
There are about 1,800 financial officers in the public service of Canada, and indeed the Treasury Board is very much in agreement with the Auditor General that it is not enough. Too many financial management and control operations are entrusted to clerical people and people whose qualifications are often insufficient. Many departments and agencies have not yet elevated their chief financial officer to the position that he or she must occupy in the management structure in order to maintain or upgrade standards of financial adrrtinistration. This is a specific answer to the question of the Leader of the Opposition. It is my opinion, and our endeavour in almost every case-on some very small boards it might be slightly different-that this person should report not through anybody else but directly, at least, to the deputy minister of the department, the chairman of a board of the president of a Crown corporation.

Economic Policy

In finishing, I would like to emphasize-and re-emphasize perhaps for the hundredth time-that the appointment by the government of the Royal Commission of Inquiry on Financial Organization and Accountability was not intended to pre-empt the report of the Auditor General. The Leader of the Opposition raised the question of the Glassco commission, and in some ways I agree with some of the implications of his comments as I interpreted them. I think we all recall that the Glassco commission emphasized in its report the importance of what it called "the essential safeguards" operating independently of the framework of management placed under the authority of ministers-the Public Service Commission and the Auditor General. The commissioners described the function of the Auditor General in the following terms:
The other external safeguard rests with the Auditor General, in his responsibility forjudging the efficacy of government accounting systems, internal control and audit procedures and other techniques of financial management, and ensuring that public funds are adequately protected against misuse and are legally spent. This function and his duty of disclosing to parliament and the public any evidence of illegality, irresponsibility and dishonesty in the handling of money, serve as powerful deterrents.
However, a crucial element of the Glassco commission's approach to public administration has been generally overlooked in the debate which followed the appointment of the royal commission the other day, because the Glassco commission stressed in the strongest terms that the first and primary guarantee of administrative integrity was the new concept of

management it proposed, with its emphasis on a much sharper definition of responsibility, authority and accountability.

To continue my comments on the Glassco commission, I think hon. members are aware that over the past ten years managerial responsibility and authority certainly have been effectively decentralized in the public service and entrusted to deputy ministers and heads of other government agencies. The fact is-and this is the fundamental point which we as parliamentarians have to examine very carefully, and I accept the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition that it might be done in a non-partisan way-that in that decentralization it is quite possible, certainly in terms of financial control, and I am talking about financial control after allocation of budgets and after the spending authority has been placed in the hands of a department or agency, that the pendulum may have swung too far in the direction of decentralization-

-to the extent that the central control and leadership which I am told in the Glassco perspective were to come from the privy Council Office and the Treasury Board has not always proved as effective as the government might have wished or, indeed, as parliamentarians in this House might have wished.
A major stumbling-block has been the difficulty the government has encountered in really building that third leg of the managerial concept proposed by the Glassco commission, which was administrative accountability. In other words, the delegation of responsibility and authority to managers could only work if those managers could be held accountable for their actions and decisions, and the Glassco commission, unfortunately-as I see it, with hindsight-considered as being beyond its terms of reference the identification of any system which a parliamentary government might adopt to fulfill this further requirement of administrative integrity.
I noted in the November 22 statement I made that the views of the Glassco commission on the political character of public administration were idealistic and, I think, overoptimistic and perhaps even somewhat simplistic. The commission concluded by saying this:
In the last analysis there cannot be any precise formal division of authority between ministers and their officials. Their partnership must depend on the existence of suitable working arrangements for which no legislative blueprint can be drawn.
The fact of the matter is-and I can at least say this to hon. members in this House-that in the view of the government these working arrangements do not always work that well and
December 9, 1976

that some explicit administrative or legislative framework might have to be established to implement effectively this principle of accountability. That is one of the major factors which led us to establish the royal commission of inquiry, and the examination by the government of these issues was, of course, significantly influenced by the views expressed on several occasions in the past years by the auditor general. But most certainly, whether hon. members want to accept it or not, our intention was certainly not to launch an inquiry on the inquiries of the auditor general. Rather, we felt that that principle of accountability-and it is just related to the placement in the structure of a potential comptroller-general; there are other issues here which are important to examine-as well as some of the recommendations made by the Auditor General pertaining to accountability, had to be more comprehensively reviewed, and that examination of their constitutional, political and broader administrative aspects was well beyond the mandate of the Auditor General-and he himself was one of the first to say so in his report and in subsequent comments he has made publicly in the past weeks.
We also thought that the considered views of royal commissioners are required at this stage to reconcile best the principle of ministerial responsibility with that of accountability and so to protect the duties and prerogatives of parliament against the possibility of bureaucratic encroachment. Some of the suggestions I have heard made in this House in recent days-and I know they are made in the heat of political exchange-come close to challenging the responsibility of ministers of this House for what happens in their departments, or asking whether we should switch this responsibility to identified public servants. Both options should be examined, but we should fully understand the implications of what happens. 1 know that the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) is very eager to get the AECL and all the rest aboard, but it is time, particularly in light of those kinds of incidents, that we had a better financial link, better financial control and a better financial system to make sure that we have these things under control.
