speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although the smothering words of the minister are not instructive and on point, the fact that we have this motion before us today in itself constitutes evidence of the strong, serious and always urgent concern felt by Canadians about the financial mismanagement of this government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Although the motion presented by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) is broken down into three or four specifics, in its essentials it deals with an over-all criticism of the financial operations of this government. As such, it is remarkably similar to a motion I put forward a week ago on behalf of the New Democratic Party, which was supported by the official opposition. During the interim this government has not moved at all to show it is concerned with the questions related to financial mismanagement that have been posed virtually every day since that debate. Today, our party will give its unequivocal support to the motion before the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Last week I drew attention to the need for this government to appoint a comptroller immediately, as recommended in the most recent Auditor General's report. The minister who spoke on behalf of the government at that time did not deal with that proposal. He used up all his time speaking on totally erroneous and, I would say, at times immoral matters entirely unrelated to the motion. The minister who spoke for the government today did not deal with the central recommendation of the Auditor General, namely, that we have a comptroller-general. I want to say to the minister that even the news he has given today about the appointment of senior financial control officers in each department, as important and necessary as they are, is not an adequate substitute for appointing a comptroller-general as was recommended by the Auditor General. The government's arguments were so weak and so superficial in the first two days after the recommendations that the minister himself did not even have enough nerve to trot them out again today.
The second point we made in the debate last week, and referred to in the comments of the Leader of the Opposition today, was on the inadequacy of our committee system to deal with the financial supervision of the operations of this government. The mythology that surrounds parliamentary commit-
[Mr. Baldwin.)
tees is remarkable. Every member and all parties in this House know that they are a farce.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
They serve as rubber-stamps for the government of the day; that is all. They are time-consuming for members of all parties and produce virtually nothing by way of an effective contribution to legislation or supervision of government activities in the House of Commons. We might as well get rid of them entirely as maintain them in their present form.
Specifically, in terms of the motion today as with the one we proposed last week, what is required of the government, if we are to take them seriously, is to give adequate staff and a real research capacity to the committees so that members of the opposition or the government, when they deal with important matters, have the intellectual and factual resources necessary to do an adequate job. The kind of operations that the public accounts committee of this House is expected to conduct cannot be done with the scandalous resources put at its disposal. I repeat the point made a week ago: if our committees are to perform an essential and important function in the parliament of Canada, namely, the supervision of the financial operations of this government, they need to be re-equipped and to be given adequate staff to do the job.
While reiterating our strong belief in the need for immediate corrective action in those two areas, in the comptroller-general area and the staffing of committees, and giving our general support to the motion, I want this afternoon to talk specifically about the serious need for tightening the supervisory financial control over our Crown corporations in general and over AECL in particular. The House will recall that the Auditor General could not have made a more scathing condemnation of our Crown corporations if he had deliberately set out to do so in his selection of facts. In his report, the Auditor General made several recommendations and came to certain conclusions. He found that Crown corporations which, from the perspective of members of parliament, ought to act as models in a Canadian community in setting standards of efficiency and moral propriety which the private sector should imitate, have unfortunately acted in a contrary manner. That is what the Auditor General discovered.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The Auditor General reached several conclusions about our Crown corporations; and we did not hear the minister either last week or this week in replying deal with the specifics of the criticism-and that, too, is disgraceful. What are the criticisms of the Auditor General? First, there is no central agency in the government whose exclusive purpose
December 9, 1976

it is to identify all corporations owned and controlled by the government of Canada. Such agency does not exist. Second, he concluded that the private sector in Canada is subject to a greater degree of control with respect to its operations than this country's Crown corporations. Third, the annual deficits of our Crown corporations are regularly and systematically understated. The fourth, and most important, point given the nature of today's debate is that parliament itself is given incomplete information on the financial position and practices of Crown corporations over which we ought to exercise supervisory authority. To repeat, that description of this government's behaviour, of its attitude to its major obligations and our Crown corporations, is a disgrace.
Instead of ignoring such criticism, ministers of the Crown should be on their feet answering. If they disagree in detail, they ought to say, "We disagree with the details of the criticism, but we shall get on with the job of correcting errors." There has been no indication in statements made today, in those made in the last two weeks or in answers made during the question period that the cabinet cares one whit about the criticism the Auditor General made of government mismanagement of the Crown corporations of Canada.
Recent horror stories-I use those words with care-about a number of Crown corporations fully document and substantiate the Auditor General's description of the operations of our Crown corporations. Let me list some of the items which recently came to light. I shall mention four examples to show the behaviour of Crown corporations, behaviour which ought to concern Canadians greatly. The first example concerns Polysar. Serious allegations were made by the former auditor general, Mr. Maxwell Henderson, that Polysar Limited, a Crown corporation, had paid rebates to some European companies in the form of special deposits to special kinds of bank accounts. From the available evidence, those so-called rebates involved either bribes or facilitated the violation of the tax laws of other countries whose governments would expect the government of Canada to set a much higher standard of conduct.
The second example concerns the operations of AECL in South Korea. Payments totalling more than $15 million were made to one Saul Eisenberg, the owner of United Developments Limited and other companies associated with Mr. Eisenberg, in connection with the attempt to sell a CAN DU reactor to South Korea. The Auditor General reported that in his opinion the documentation for these kinds of payments was inadequate-that is some euphemism! Subsequent testimony given before the public accounts committee indicates that the payments for so-called consultants of various kinds, for which Mr. Eisenberg submitted inadequately detailed invoices, were in fact payments to Mr. Eisenberg's own companies in various countries operating under a variety of names. One wonders why he would want to operate a number of companies under a variety of names, and why would he get a variety of payments for the same work? To ask the question is to suggest the answer, as members on both sides of the House recognize.
Economic Policy
The third case involves the AECL attempt to sell a CAN DU reactor in Argentina. Payment was made by AECL to a numbered Swiss bank account of $2.4 million as its portion of a commission payable to an agent for "services rendered over an extended period." Investigations concerning the possibility of bribery involving those funds provided by the people of Canada through the government of Canada are now under way in Argentina. That is a serious matter; yet when the minister responsible was asked just a week ago in the House if he had been in touch with the man in charge of the bribery investigation involving Canadian funds in Argentina, the minister said no, he had not personally been in touch with him but understood that the head of AECL had been in communication with him in some way, perhaps by telephone or letter.
As I say, he understood that AECL had been in touch with the man in Argentina now investigating possible bribery involving Canadian funds. Mr. Speaker, that response was totally inadequate. The minister involved should not simply have "understood" that the head of AECL had been in touch with the man conducting that investigation. The minister himself ought to have been in touch, and pursuing as thoroughly as he could, investigations being conducted in Argentina.
The fourth example concerns Canadian Commercial Corporation. Mr. G. R. Long, deputy auditor general under Maxwell Henderson, reported in a recent interview that he found an entry of $500,000 on the books of the Canadian Commercial Corporation in 1972 listed as "Marketing services." He states that the money went to Canadair and that it was his belief, and I quote, "that the money was used partly to pay off some Venezuelan official" in connection with the sale of 20 fighter bombers. Mr. Long commented further that "Certain payments were made, but you'll never be able to prove it." The auditors at the time were unsuccessful in their attempts to inspect the books of Canadair, a company which has subsequently come under the full public ownership of the people of Canada.
What have been some of the specific responses by ministers of the Crown directly involved in terms of their responsibility and, indeed, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)? A week ago in the House, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) said:
Commercial practices in other countries. .. sometimes are different to ours.... I am not about to condemn the morals of anybody. It would be very presumptuous for Canadians to tell other people how to conduct their morals.
That is what he said. About the same time his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), with reference to the same general set of moral misdemeanours, as I would describe them as best, said the following:
We are not in a position to impose our morality or moral values on other countries.
Then there is the Prime Minister. What did he say? In reply to a question put by myself on November 30, he said:

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy
The House might want to address itself to the question whether we want the Crown corporations to continue to be involved in business or whether they should all be privatized ...
If we want to depart from what are acceptable business, accounting and legal practices in the name of some ethical standard which we may well want to apply,
I suggest that we should get out of the bussiness of having Crown corporations.
That is what the Prime Minister of this country had to say. The minister directly responsible, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and the Prime Minister all indicated an attitude of moral indifference. A renowned scholar of this century, Hannah Arendt, a woman who died not long ago, used the illuminating phrase "The banality of evil". I suggest that the response to the recent revelations of the international behaviour of Crown corporations by the Prime Minister and senior ministers of the Crown is certainly banal and comes dangerously close to being evil.
The Prime Minister and his ministers are, at best, remaining benignly indifferent to such practices that deeply disturbed the former auditor general. In my view, such a response offers implicit moral support of their continuance. I ask, in all seriousness, whether there is any possible interpretation to be drawn from the statements they made other than they are prepared to accept in other countries moral behaviour for Canadian corporations, private or publicly owned, which they would not accept at home. Therefore, they are implicity saying-

Mr. Speaker, I thank the members of the House for their consideration. In taking this attitude, the Prime Minister and ministers of the Crown are implicitly accepting a double standard of morality. They are implicitly telling Canadian corporations to continue with these operations. In 1968, Gunnar Myrdal, the Swedish economist, devoted a great deal of space in his book "Asian Drama" to the problem of the behaviour of businessmen in the third world. He concluded with the following observation:
A western firm operating in a South Asian country often finds it convenient. .. to give a negotiated lump sum to a more or less professional briber, an "agent" who then undertakes to pay off all those whose co-operation is necessary for the smooth conduct of production and business.
This describes perfectly the practice that appears to have gone on with AECL in both South Korea and Argentina, Earn sorry to say. Since the practice is common and has gone on for so long, any protestations from the government that they were unaware of what their agents were doing to earn their money severely tests the credulity of all members of parliament and the public of Canada. This is especially so since the advice to Canadian businessmen which the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was giving in 1973 clearly documents that they were aware of these dubious practices. In 1973, that department published a booklet entitled "The Nigerian

Market: A Survey of Current Opportunities". Part of the advice to Canadian businessmen contained in this little gem of a booklet was the following:
Canadian companies pursuing international tendered opportunities involving either EDC (Export Development Corporation) or Cl DA (Canadian International Development Agency) financing support should ensure that they have between 5 per cent and 8 per cent in their bid price to cover the necessary marketing and public relations costs associated with doing business in Nigeria (i.e., often more than one agent and/or "representative" is needed to win an international tender).
It is time for an unequivocal declaration, not from one of the appropriate ministers but the Prime Minister that the government of Canada expects Canadian corporations, private or public, to comply with the highest moral and legal standards, not only at home but abroad.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INEPT HANDLING OF ECONOMIC POLICY BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Leadership is precisely what is required now in this matter, and it is leadership that is precisely what is lacking. In my view, Canadians will not accept the spurious and-I will say it-immoral answers already implied by the Prime Minister when answering in the House on this matter. His answer amounts to saying, "Others do it; therefore, we must join in". That is the logic of his position. The first thing to be said about this is that a wrong is a wrong is a wrong. It does not acquire virtue by being repeated by others. The second point I would make, and this is important given the kinds of general observations that have been made about business practice both in Canada and abroad, is as follows: there are many, many companies-I would like to think, a majority of them-both Canadian and foreign which will not have anything to do with the kind of practices we have heard so much about in recent days.
We are aware that competitors of Polysar from West Germany and the United States refused to indulge in the kind of practices with which Polysar has been so preoccupied and which were so thoroughly and, unfortunately in terms of their implications, documented by the Auditor General. The point is, it is not necessary to be corrupt-and that is what you have to be if you are offering bribes. It is not necessary to practice that kind of behaviour in order to get business abroad. What you must do is compete. You must market a product which merits purchase by other countries, and produce salesmen who are honest and technically competent to sell those products abroad. The contracts will follow. That is what General Electric says it is doing in the United States. It is time the Crown corporations began practising the same kind of high ethical standards. It is time they got the leadership where it counts, and that is from the Prime Minister.
In the view of the New Democratic Party, the Prime Minister has an obligation to put guidelines before the House soon outlining the minimum legal and moral standards he expects Crown corporations to abide by both at home and abroad. Second, he should ensure, through the House leader and other appropriate steps, that the committees of the House
December 9, 1976

of Commons will be given, as a matter of right, the task of investigating the annual reports of all Crown corporations as they are submitted to the government. That would be one effective way of ensuring that members of this House would have a continuing supervisory role, at least, to play in ensuring that Crown corporations do the kind of job for Canadians that Canadians expect of them.
All 1 can say on behalf of my party, in response to the indifference, at best, on the part of the government toward the serious state of moral morass which has been outlined is: enough is enough; it is time to clean house. I, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by adding thereto immediately after the words "in the handling of the public finances of Canada", the following words:
"particularly its failure to establish mechanisms to achieve effective supervisory financial control over Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and other Crown
corporations."

I would go further than that, Mr. Speaker. In view of the reaction to the lack of any sense of morality on the part of that minister, supported to a certain extent by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), surely we have to ask ourselves whether this is the type of minister who should be heading up the portfolio of industry, trade and commerce. Is it right to have one of the most senior persons in this government in the portfolio of industry, trade and commerce in view of the questionable moral judgment that he has shown in this House? Would we not be right in asking for the resignation of this minister, bearing in mind that he should be setting the standard for industry? I would say that certain of the actions taken by Crown corporations are a reflection on Canada's good corporate image around the world. I should also like to refer to an editorial that appeared in the Toronto Star headlined, "Would you lie to make a dollar?". The editorial commences:
Jean Chretien is right when he says the government has no business in setting out the business ethics of other nations. If they think bribes and hidden payments are all right, it's entirely their business.
But he is wrong, when he says Canada's Crown corporations should go along if shady ethics are requested by a foreign customer . . . The issue is not whether Canada should tell other countries "how to conduct their morals". The question is how are we to conduct our own ... That, I suggest, is a fairly uniform condemnation of the minister's statements and is the general impression left by this government in regard to this very important issue. Unfortunately, I was disappointed today to hear the Prime Minister's still adamant reply when he was questioned on this general topic. In the House this afternoon he stated:
We expect that the officials of Canada and the officials of Crown corporations will behave and conduct themselves according to law. This is a general position.
Should there be any serious suggestion that any official of this government or of any Crown corporation will not conduct themselves according to law? What about the much broader question, Mr. Speaker? What are they expected to do when it comes to morality? Is it enough simply to say that because Polysar conveniently has a Crown corporation in Switzerland, and in turn another corporation has, I suggest, a Crown corporation in Netherlands Antilles, it is sufficient for us to say that this is all perfectly legal, that you can shift funds around and evade taxation, all perfectly legally? At the same time, if Polysar tried to do exactly the same thing here in Canada it would be illegal and wrong. That is exactly what we are talking about here.
This Polysar setup has been structured so that it has a subsidiary in Switzerland and in the Netherlands Antilles. That kind of a structure provides a relief not only in the Polysar situation, but in respect of any little corporation that wants to get into these rinky-dink deals. It is going to provide relief through the government's Bill C-12 which ratifies an agreement with Switzerland for the avoidance of double taxation, thereby facilitating the type of tax dodge we have been talking about in this House for several days.
This is an example of the inconsistency of this government. It acknowledged that it wants things tightened up and that we should have some new guidelines, and on the other hand it proposed that this House ratify a treaty with Switzerland. This will facilitate the use of numbered accounts in Switzerland, making Switzerland a tax haven beyond dreams.
There will be no need, for example, to use the Netherlands, Antilles anymore. One can go directly to Switzerland and maintain direct contact there with whichever corporation you wish to deal. speechtext:
I am very pleased to have the opportunity of making a few brief comments today on the motion now before us. There is no question but that it is an important motion. It does in fact go to the heart of a question that is of a great deal of concern not only to members of parliament but to the public generally.
If I may, I should like just for a moment to indicate that as a Liberal member of parliament I think I have demonstrated over the years since 1968 that I have had a long-standing and genuine interest in public expenditures. In my experience on the Public Accounts Committee from 1968 to 1972 I spent a great deal of time in a very independent way, like many members did at that time, dealing with a lot of questions, not the least of which was the Bonaventure inquiry, in respect of which I played a very significant role. I think hon. members will acknowledge that.
The fact of the matter is that I am not one who is going to bring forward excuses for the government, allowing it to continue in a way that would not adequately protect the public purse. There is no question in my mind that we, as the government and as parliamentarians, have to turn our eyes inward occasionally, and begin to to look very carefully at levels of public expenditure, and the way in which those expenditures are controlled.
First of all in respect of levels of expenditures, in this area there is certainly a great deal of parliamentary control. Members may have complaints as to the amount of opportunity they have to debate the estimates and so on, but there is no question that all of us do have these opportunities and that parliament itself does control these global expenditures.
In respect of such global expenditures, aside from the fact that they are controlled in global ways, there are legitimate concerns in connection with the detailed application of budgets and estimates when it gets down to the individual department or Crown corporation. In the global context, the government has announced varying policies on a number of occasions intended to make significant cuts in the growth of public expenditure in Canada. Budgets have been curtailed and policies have been changed. I think this is all for the good. We all support such measures.
Let me make a suggestion which I think might assist us in terms of actually controlling the level of expenditure in a budgetary way. It is my belief that the government ought to conduct a very serious and high level profile cost-benefit analysis of all government programs, departments, and agencies so that we can assure ourselves that every dollar we spend is in fact returning the best possible result.
It goes without saying that parliaments spend a great deal of time bringing forward new laws and far too little time looking at them after they have been brought forward. I believe it is in
[Mr. Roy (Timmins).J
the public interest that we sit down and correctly analyze all the programs of the government to ensure they are performing the purposes for which they were originally intended, and that the need for these programs still remains, or whether we in fact believe that in a priority way the money could be better spent in another direction, in which case these programs should be reduced or scrapped altogether. If that kind of approach were taken in conjunction with the top executives, businessmen and other specialists in the country brought in to assist us in such an analysis, I think we would restore a great deal of confidence in the budgetary process of the Government of Canada. In addition to this, I think we have to do more.
We must address ourselves to many of the legitimate points brought to our attention by the Auditor General. The motion before us reads in part:
... deplores the fact that key recommendations of the Auditor General will not be implemented in the foreseeable future . . .
Surely that is one of the essential elements that we are talking about today. Yet, listening to speeches prior to that time, particularly from the other side, I heard very little reference to the key proposals of the Auditor General. What are the key proposals?

I think that should be recognized in all fairness by all members of the House.
Let us get down-now that that has been laid to rest, I hope successfully for the moment-to some other detailed observations that hon. members have made on the Auditor General's report.
Much has been said about bottom line accounting, about the need to control government expenditures in an accounting way, as you would control General Motors. There is no question that the government has no excuse for not doing precisely that in specific terms. However, 1 would draw to the attention of hon. members that we do not operate, nor can any government operate, simply and exclusively on bottom line accounting. It is not always a question of saving money. We can save a lot of money. All we have to do is to cut out all the cost-sharing programs, and you have cut the budget by a phenomenal amount. Saving money is not really the question. The question is not to waste it, and not to spend it in areas where the public is not best served by having it spent in those areas. That requires a value judgment; it requires us to sit down and carefully sift the priorities of the people of this country and decide what programs will be scrapped and which ones will be retained.
I would like to draw to your attention, and use an illustration in respect of this, that it is not always simply a question of accounting. I will give you an example. Some of us have addressed ourselves to the question of space allocations to car rental agencies in airports across Canada. The government established a certain tendering process which brought forward certain winners and certain losers. The government had an option not to accept winning tenders on the basis that it felt that if it rejected a winner and accepted a loser, it would maximize government revenue. That sounds perfectly consistent with what everyone is talking about here today. But is it really consistent with good government policy? I say not, because the maximization of revenue is not everything. It is not the be all and end all of everything.
The fact of the matter is that the policy, as I view it, was designed to give a certain kind of guaranteed location to Canadian operators against international and multinational competition. That is good. If that were not part of the policy, then clearly we would have just allowed bids to come in and would take the top ones, which would maximize revenue to the extreme, but probably we would not have any Canadians doing
Economic Policy
business in Canadian airports. 1 do not think that is desirable, and I doubt if anybody thinks it is. Surely that point illustrates that it is not always exclusively a question of dollars and cents. If that had been done, we may well have ended up with another observation by the Auditor General.
The second point in respect of the horror stories which people have addressed themselves to is the question relating to the Atomic Energy Commission and all the veiled suggestions of bribery, corruption, and so on. I do not think there has been one member who spoke on the subject so far today who is a member of the Public Accounts Committee which addressed itself to the question. I rather doubt if any responsible member of parliament who sits on that committee would be making those kinds of statements and, if they did, they would be the first ones to realize those statements were not founded in fact. If they are in the future, fine, I am all for pulling that kind of information out and getting down to the root of it, but there is nothing at present that suggests that. The Auditor General does not suggest it, nor has anyone responsible suggested it. It happens, perhaps, to suit the political purpose of some people who are not nervous about being irresponsible.

speechtext: You must be smiling when you say that.

speechtext: Let us have a look at the question. The simple facts relating to the Atomic Energy Commission problem and the sale of a reactor to Korea are very simply put. Hon. members ask, "why an agent?" That question was not brought before the Public Accounts Committee, although it may be a legitimate question. In fact I think it is a legitimate question, although in the Public Accounts Committee it would be an irrelevant question. However, that would not prevent hon. members opposite from pursuing it in any event.
It seems to me that to answer the question as to why there was an agent, one would have to have a great wealth of background information as to how such international contracts are made, how it is traditionally done, and if it is possible for a Crown corporation to do it directly without an agency arrangement. Some would say it is possible, but there is no doubt that it would require the setting up of a whole new department of a corporation to deal with it. Then of course we could end up with the charge that it cost perhaps $25 million because it was done in-house rather than through an agency. I am not one who looks into a crystal ball and who would know what the net benefits or disadvantages would be to do it alone. I only know that General Motors does not generally peddle its cars through its own dealerships. It does its business in a different way.
I was once in business. I employed salesmen from time to time, not only across Canada but also in other countries, and I

must say that my auditor never once asked me what the expenses of my commissioned salesmen were because we could not care less. We just paid them their commissions, and that was it. That is a very simple concept even for hon. members opposite to understand, and I am sure that in the business experience of those who have any-and it may be limited- surely they themselves have worked under that kind of arrangement.

I must admit that I have not covered all the points I had intended to cover, but I will conclude by saying that the Auditor General, Mr. Macdonell, is a man of superb qualifications, tremendous integrity, and honesty. The President of the Treasury Board has responded in a magnificent way, and with the probing and vigilance of members of parliament to ensure that we get a better handle on public expenditures, and with the pressure exerted by the press and the people of this country, I have no doubt at all that we will serve the people of this country well by making the needed adjustments and changes in our method of controlling expenditures. Mr. Speaker, supported by the substantial segment of the Conservative party present in this Chamber, I intend to make a few truths known to government supporters.
Just before the House adjourned at six o'clock 1 was in deep shock. I had listened to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), a man for whom I have respect, and consider intelligent, say before he concluded his remarks that the actions of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited had been beyond challenge, and that what they had done ought to meet with the "Good Housekeeping" seal of government approval. He suggested that they deserve commendation from the public of Canada for what they had done. I was amazed.
Half way through his speech he asked why we, the opposition, had brought forward the present motion. Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had followed me around the country these past ten days he would know why. I have been in many parts of Canada, in four or five cities and various areas, have travelled by aircraft, train and automobile, and talked to a great many people. Let me tell my hon. friends opposite, sitting smug in their complacency and proud of what they have done, that the people of this country are aroused about the issue, are aroused about the extent to which the government has permitted, condoned, I suspect even encouraged Crown corporations and probably others to engage in a series of practices which have put us in a difficult position. Government members can say that it was not of their doing. To that I say. "He who lies down with a dog gets up with fleas."

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Obviously that applies to many members of the opposition.

The people are outraged about what has happened. It may well be that such conduct is prevalent among private corporations and individuals. 1 make no comment on that. 1 used to make a living defending people charged with criminal offences. If they were caught and found guilty, they were punished; that was the law. But, Mr. Speaker, we are speaking of Crown corporations under the control and domination of the government. The government is answerable for them through a minister to this House, and through this House to the people of Canada. Mr. Speaker, how can members on the government side, particularly ministers of the Crown, stand up in this House and say, "Yes, what was done was perfectly all right. We condoned it. When you go into another country, you adopt their morals and do the things they do." I challenge that as a theory of government. It is not acceptable to this House, nor to the people of this land.

Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member accept a question?
Economic Policy
Yes, Mr. Speaker, but only so long as the time is taken into account; only so long as the time the hon. member takes is not taken off my time.
I will keep track of the time. This is supposed to be a debating House and I am interested in what the hon. member has to say.

Mr. Speaker, I thought I heard the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) say that the government controlled Crown corporations. I would ask him whether he is suggesting that the government does control or should in fact recapture control of Crown corporations.
Mr. Speaker, that is not the issue; when it arises, I will deal with it.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The hon. member is speaking out of both sides of his mouth.

One of the facts of life is that the government, with the acquiescence of the majority of its members, can control Crown corporations through this House, whenever it wants to do so. It can do that at any time.
What about through the committees?

The hon. member is being facetious about committees. Our committee system, by virtue of the way the government runs it, has become nothing but a farce. The government, through the incestuous relationship between heads of committees-
Rubbish!

The hon. member can make his own speech later, if he so wishes. As I was saying, there is politically and intellectually an incestuous relationship between the heads of these committees and agencies. We have witnessed a steady procession of such people. They have been appointed as the heads of agencies, then entered the government service, then private industry, and back again. There is no doubt in my mind that, at least indirectly, the government controls many of these corporations, knows what they are doing, and condones their actions. If the hon. member does not believe that, he is not as smart as I think he is.
Are you saying that we are breaking the law of this country?
Order, please. I suggest to hon. members that we are debating a specific motion, and I suggest that hon. members adhere to the terms of the motion.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Hon. members opposite are repeating the same old things.

Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member permit a question? I ask what his great party did with regard to those corporations between 1958 and 1962? What kind of job did

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy
the hon. member's party do during that time with regard to this question?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The hon. member does not have to answer that question. Everybody knows the answer.
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member's only defence is to resort to conditions which existed 15 or 20 years ago, that is pitiful.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Shameful.

Mr. Speaker, most of these Crown corporations were established by the government. The relationship between the heads of the Crown corporations and the government is well known, indeed notorious. There is no question about it. I suggest that not a thing passes within the head offices of these Crown corporations of which the government is unaware. Probably it encourages them to engage in these activities. I say to the government, it is your responsibility.
But I asked a question.

Well, they are your children. There should have been an abortion a long time ago, before they became your children.
Having disposed of these silly interruptions, I shall continue with the debate. The hon. member for Ontario asked why we have brought forward the present motion. I say, ask the people of Canada what they think about this situation; what is on their minds as a result of what they have read, seen, and witnessed concerning the conduct of these Crown corporations. These corporations are the responsibility of the government. I say that the government was aware of what was happening. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) received a letter three and a half years ago in one case. 1 shall return to it later. So, do not pretend that the government was not aware of what was going on. It is a sickening situation, for public morality is the issue which may ultimately destroy the system under which we live. If we do not govern our conduct with a reasonable and sensible measure of morality, our system will no more survive than the lines children draw in the sand will survive when the tide comes in. Let hon. members opposite remember that when they support their government. In the view of the Prime Minister and ministers, what was done by AECL, Polymer and other Crown corporations was fine and good and, as the hon. member for Ontario suggested, deserved support. If that is the view of hon. members opposite, then it is high time this country was rid of this government. Let us return to decent morality.
Let me in a couple of sentences trace the ancestry of this particular motion now before the House. Year after year my party and the NDP to my left, as well as the Creditistes, either brought forward or supported similar motions. They were motions demanding that the government deal strongly and firmly with the question of parliamentary control of the expenditures of this government, and control the spending without restraint of taxpayers' money taken by the government. This has been going on year after year. I have here a list of the
[Mr. Boulanger.)
various motions, some of which I will deal with. Some of my colleagues will deal with others. In 1970 there was a motion in the name of the then leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Halifax, (Mr. Stanfield), almost in the same terms as this. In 1972 there was a motion in my name:
That this House, noting the continuing erosion of Parliament's control over government spending of public moneys . . . reaffirms the fundamental principle of the Canadian constitution
There was another motion in 1973, and one in 1974. We took this action and got no results. We took the only method within our capacity. No action was taken. The government did not pay any attention to the issues we brought before it. We documented the issues, chapter and verse. We called to its attention the problems that compelled us as responsible members of this House to deal with these issues. The government did not do anything.
We brought this action, reinforced in our right to do so by actions of the government in condoning and approving what has now been disclosed to the public as being the unconscionable action of these Crown corporations. It is all very well for my friends opposite to say fine, we have to sell the CAN DU reactors and therefore it is quite proper to be involved in irregularities, bribery, and corruption to do that. Some of us do not believe reactors should have been sold in the first place, and some of us do not believe they should have been sold to the countries they were. But let us forget that. This kind of mechanism was sold to these countries, and sold with the aid of inducements, bribery, and corruption. This has been reinforced by evidence given by the Auditor General before the Public Accounts Committee. It is time that this House and this country took notice.
Hear, hear!

The present Auditor General said in his report that the government has lost control over spending. That is quite obvious. The previous auditor general said, year after year, in his annual reports that parliament had lost control. He said that in 1967, 1968, 1969 and 1970. In his last report before leaving his job because of age, at page 11 of the 1972 Auditor General's report, the previous Auditor General said, and I quote:
What I do question and deem it my duty to draw to the attention of the House are the increasing tendencies displayed by the Treasury Board and its staff to devote their energies and resources towards circumventing parliamentary control rather than towards improving the efficiency of departmental and agency operations by remedying situations which for years have demanded attention.
That statement by the previous Auditor General is as true today as it was then. Nothing that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) said today gives me any feeling of relief that the situation will be changed.
Hear, hear!

It so happens that there was a motion in 1973 on this issue. The hon. member responsible for the government was the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), then the
December 9, 1976

President of the Treasury Board. As reported at page 4016 of Hansard, first session, volume 4, 1973, the hon. member made this comment:
I said that the new form
That is the new form of looking after, caring for and examining the public accounts.
-would include much more information about Crown corporations than had been included in the past.
That was a few weeks after the then President of the Treasury Board received from the Prime Minister a letter pointing out that Polymer Corporation was engaged in tactics which, in the words of the Prime Minister, were likely to prove very embarrassing. That is a clear hint they were known to the Prime Minister to be improper. He made that statement in his letter to the then President of the Treasury Board.
The President of the Treasury Board then got on the telephone and called Mr. Hampson, one of the great friends of the party, and said, "Look, Mr. Hampson, things are not going right. I have a letter from the Prime Minister. Can you tell me what is going on?". Mr. Hampson said that these practices were being carried on by private corporations, and why should we not do the same? In their desire to carry on selling, without regard to propriety, morals, or the feelings of the people of Canada, they forgot all about it.
Three of four weeks later the then President of the Treasury Board stood in this House and said; "We are taking steps to tighten up the financial procedures of Crown corporations." He did not do a damm thing from then until now, three and one half years later. That is a clear indication of the low degree of fiscal morality which has pervaded this government and, unfortunately, members opposite who support them.
Hear, hear!

My time is nearly up, Mr. Speaker. It is a difficult situation, a problem we have to contend with. We have to develop a state of openness in our society. We have to persuade the public, the taxpayers, the consumers, and the voters of Canada, that it is possible to have decency and honesty in government and in the carrying out of the duties of this parliament.
There are many things that can be done. 1 suggest, within the terms of the motion that we are considering, a declaration by this government which will be supported unanimously from all parts of the House, that it will introduce a measure providing for openness and freedom of information so that the actions that are committed and the wrongs that are done will be made known. That would do a great deal to persuade the public that there is developing a much better degree of morality. It will not be the milfenium. 1 do not suggest that. However, after a great many years involved in the practice of law, sitting in this House, and in other political public endeavours, 1 believe that if people know that what they write and what they do will in due course be made public, it will have a very refreshing and wholesome effect on what they do.
Economic Policy
The kinds of things we have been dealing with in this House and the kinds of things the Auditor General mentioned in his reports will not vanish. From what I know of human nature, that is too much to hope. However, they will diminish to at least an acceptable state in this country. We will again be able to be proud. Canadians will be able to go abroad knowing that they have an open, decent society in Canada, a situation which does not exist in government circles today.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as 1 read the confused motion which is before us tonight, I see that it combines many items. It talks about the House being deprived of its genuine role in the discussion of estimates, secrecy in studies, and deplores the fact that recommendations-

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It is an opposition motion.

Yes, and I am pointing out that it is a confused motion. I am trying to analyze its import. It condemns the government for inept handling of public finances.
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) moved an amendment bringing in Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. If there is a common element in the various items brought here, it is an attack on the government's management of government business.
Very good.

Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal with some fundamental things in a way I had expected members on the opposite side to deal with them. They talked about estimates. We heard the old story about the golden age of this House when we had estimates brought before it and you could do things. 1 sat in this House. I saw the estimates and not one line was changed. One side lined up against the other side in an interminable debate. There were many Speaker's rulings. It was a disgrace. There was no golden age existing at some time in the past.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is just as disgraceful now.

If hon. members will bear with me I think they will find that what 1 have to say is interesting. If they wish to study the operations of the Government of Canada they have to go back, as the Auditor General has done, to the Glassco recommendations and the way in which they were implemented.
The Auditor General was very methodical and systematic. 1 want to pay my tribute to him and commend him as a man of great integrity and great ability, a man with infinite patience and a sense of humour. 1 am confident that his recommendations will be implemented. The difference between the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and that senior official is simply one promotion for one man in the Treasury Board, and the reommendation of the Auditor General for a

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy
Comptroller General, or whatever it is, will be implemented. I am confident that this key recommendation will be accepted by the government because it is a very logical thing to do.
On the financial side, those of us who sat on the committee and listened to the testimony agree that one of the major responsibilities of the Royal commission which has been named is to look into the whole operation of Crown corporations. We recognize, following the revelations in the Auditor General's report, that there are weaknesses. Every member of the House does. One of the great things about serving on the Public Accounts Committee is that it has a tradition of being non-partisan in these matters. The members concerned have looked sincerely at the recommendations of the Auditor General, and members on this side of the House have been among the most active in criticizing the waste and maladministration which the Auditor General has disclosed.
I propose to develop some other items tonight, Mr. Speaker. Whoever wants to study the Glassco recommendations could profit a great deal. The recommendations made sense, but the way they were implemented did not make sense. Financial controls were virtually abolished when the office of the Comptroller of the Treasury was abolished in 1969. But something else happened at the same time which was equally important and which we must bear in mind when assessing the effectiveness of the government's operations. I am referring to what was done on the delegated authority side and with regard to hiring.
At that time the philosophy was: Let the deputy ministers manage; give them the authority; free them from all these bureaucratic restraints which are hampering their efficiency. Mr. Speaker, I think it is time we took a hard look at what happened when they got free of those restraints. The Auditor General has given us the story on the expenditure side, chapter and verse-there were no financial control officers, there were no financial control manuals in the departments; no one was concerned with the process of training and recruiting and developing competent personnel. All this has been outlined.
Hon. members talk about secrecy of information. I have listened to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) many times and I have a great deal of sympathy for his point of view. But if he were to read a lot of the information which is already available to him it is surprising what he would find.
You bet!

For example, 1 have here an extract from the Annual Report of the Public Service Commission of Canada for 1974. I am reading from pages 16 and 17.
Delegation of staffing authority to departments has meant that the PSC has had to develop methods to scrutinize departmental staffing and insure that the merit principle is upheld. Auditing is carried out at headquarters and in all regional offices.
Let us review what happened when an audit took place. The report states:
Auditors review departmental appointments on a random sample and on a selected and problem-oriented basis. In the first ten months of 1974, they audited 7,082 departmental appointments out of 74,980 made. These audits
(Mr. Francis.]
revealed 1,946 departmental infractions of the Public Service Employment Act and regulations. The audits also showed that departments made 2,754 errors in carrying out directives or administrative requirements of the PSC.
Then the PSC attempted to develop a system of evaluating the quality of staff. Another audit indicated that in the first ten months 25.2 per cent of appointments audited contained infractions. Twenty departments had an infraction rate higher than this national average, and 24 departments had a lower rate.
It does not take much imagination to prompt the question: what has happened in this field of delegated authority, the scope of delegated authority when it comes to departmental appointments? Members of this House do their work as they attend committees and avail themselves of the opportunity to ask questions. The Public Service Commission is a fascinating organization to examine at this point. 1 welcome every opportunity I have to ask the chairman questions, and the last opportunity I had was on Thursday, December 2, 1976, when he appeared before the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee. Actually I was just getting at the heart of it when my ten minutes were up. Here is an extract from the record of the committee proceedings.
1 asked Mr. Gallant, the Chairman of the Public Service Commission, this question:
When a vacancy exists in the Public Service, is there any statutory requirement that the vacancy be reported to the Public Service Commission?
To which the chairman replied:
There is no requirement that the vacancy itself be reported to the Commission. There can be no appointment, however, to the position unless it is under delegated authority, without the Commission being directly involved.
If the Public Service Commission does not know where these vacancies are, I do not understand how it can do its job and carry out its responsibility for staffing and making sure the merit principle is upheld. 1 put this question to Public Service Commission personnel and they said "Each spring we send out recruiting officers to interview bright, young graduates, and draw attention to the promising careers available to them in the public service." But, Mr. Speaker, those staffing officers do not know where the vacancies are, either at present or projected. All they could do was give general encouragement.
If hon. members are really interested in the operations of the Government in Canada and not in just repeating all the things we have heard about the government hiding documents, about the government being inept, repeating all those slogans adapted from the Auditor General's report, they would be more interested in the area 1 have just mentioned. As to the other aspect, corrective action is under way. But no corrective action is under way to deal with the problems which are arising under delegated authority in the Public Service.
In the period ahead we shall be dealing with amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Again a joint committee of this House and the other place laboured for over a year and brought in a report earlier this year. The government has indicated that legislation based on its recommendations will be laid before the House. At the same time there will have to be

consequential amendments made to the Public Service Employment Act, because one statute affects the other.
What I am asking is that the government give serious consideration to reviewing what has happened under the system of delegated authority, that other arm of the Glassco report. One arm was concerned with financial control, and the other with delegated authority and the freedom to hire given to deputy ministers. I believe this has been a thorn in the side of many people who have tried hard, with a sense of professional integrity, to develop careers in the public service-the uneven way in which delegated authority has been applied and the lack of adequate auditing of the results of delegated authority and, I suggest, in some instances, bureaucratic patronage and nepotism. These matters will have to be corrected.
I know that in this city of Ottawa, for example, there are a number of instances where as many as ten members of a single family work for the Post Office Department. When you find a rude clerk at a wicket, you will often find that that clerk is very confident of his position because he has a brother-in-law or somebody else in the personnel department to protect him.
The situation calls for a review of hiring practices. The situation calls for a review of delegated authority. The situation calls for a meeting with the Public Service Commission to learn what measures the Chairman of the Public Service Commission would like to see enacted in order that he can do his job. I believe that in these circumstances the Chairman of the Public Service Commission is saying in the most polite way within the rules that he is hamstrung when he cannot know where vacancies are, when delegated authority has gone too far, when he has breaches of regulations on a scale admitted by the annual report of the Public Service Commission. The government must review the operation and undertake the kind of corrective measures that are now being implemented on the financial side.
I share, Mr. Speaker, with other members of the House concern about the "horror stories" in the annual report of the Auditor General. Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, speaking of confusion, if there is any confusion in this debate it emanates from the other side of the House, particularly from the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. He tried to speak out of both sides of his mouth on this particular issue. He commended the Auditor General for bringing to light the very serious issues associated with financial management and control in the Government of Canada, the various horror stories and so on, and then he chastised the opposition for bringing the subject forward for debate. I find that rather inconsistent.
This afternoon the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) went to great lengths to describe the government's support for the Auditor General. He outlined to the House the increase in authorized man-years in support of the Auditor General. Quite frankly, we find no argument with that, but really it is not the substance of the motion. We have not chastised the government for failing to provide sufficient resources to the office of the Auditor General, both financial and in terms of manpower. We are in fact chastising the government for failing to act upon the recommendations of the Auditor General.
It is one thing to expose, Mr. Speaker, and in this regard we have really had no problem at all with this Auditor General or his predecessor. Both have consistently exposed the inadequacies, the extravagance and the waste emanating from this administration. What we are after, Mr. Speaker, is a correction of the situation, particularly at the source. That is the real issue, to establish mechanisms and ways and means of preventing these sorts of horrors from occurring.
This afternoon the minister tried to leave the impression that no money was lost, no fraud of parliament had been committed and that government was in control. He pointed out that so far as the matter of collection was concerned all we have to do is to ask the taxpayer whether or not the government has an effective collecting agency. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, it is the disbursement side of the coin with which we are really concerned. It is the control of public funds once they get into the hands of the government with which we are concerned. We must ensure that these funds are properly accounted for and properly controlled. It is that which is the issue.
The President of the Treasury Board also stated that in his view parliament does have control and the government is held accountable. Here again we see a major conflict between the President of the Treasury Board and the Auditor General. Certainly the Auditor General does not see it in that light. As a matter of fact, this is really the highlight of his latest report.
Despite all the flak that we have received from the other side of the House, it is with a considerable degree of regret that I find the House compelled once more to initiate a debate

on an issue that is so substantive, indeed so fundamental, as that which is contained in the motion which was presented by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark). I say it is with regret, because what could be more tragic than the developing mood across this country where Canadians are becoming increasingly disenchanted and disillusioned with government and with parliament, indeed with our very system of parliamentary democracy? Even worse, Mr. Speaker, anybody who thinks that the mess in our financial administration does not add to the problems of national unity, that it does not add to the cynicism, mistrust and suspicion of federal authority, is gravely mistaken.
I believe that all of us-each and every one who is associated with this House of Commons and associated with the governing of this country-no matter what political affiliations we may have, have a very major and solemn obligation to discharge. That obligation, quite frankly, involves the restoration of confidence in our system, and restoration of the people's belief that their taxes are being wisely and prudently administered. Surely that is the very core and foundation upon which responsible government can continue to exist.
Hear, hear!

I believe it is fundamental that the taxpayers' dollars, the money given to the government by the people, must be treated by the government as funds held in trust. I am sure, in addition, that the people in all regions and provinces of Canada would display a greater degree of faith in the country, and a greater degree of patriotism, if they were assured that they were being governed by a federal administration which managed its affairs in an effective and efficient manner. They would be more patriotic if they could be assured that the federal government would address itself in a responsible fashion to the real issues of regional economic disparity, and deal with the issues of the economy inflation, high unemployment, and the basic fundamental need Canadians have for an adequate supply of jobs in order to live in dignity, and in harmony with one another.
Surely these are some of the issues that are driving a wedge into our confederation. Surely the commitment to stay unified as one nation does not begin and does not end with the province of Quebec. There are other regions in this country which, too, are having very serious difficulties. One only has to look around and examine the obvious frustrations and alienations which are growing in the outer regions of our country. These issues are continuing to fester because of the failure of the federal government to act.
Hopefully in bringing this debate to the House of Commons this afternoon and evening we will be able to contribute in some small way to meeting some of these problems, first by the reminder that the issues rising in this nation are indeed urgent and serious, and not to be sneezed at as the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) who just returned to his seat has done. Surely by directing parliament's attention to these very
December 9, 1976

basic and fundamental issues we might be able collectively to come up with some answers to our pressing problems.
The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) in a very constructive speech today, I believe, brought out a matter in which I concur with him, and one which I advanced in a speech in the House on October 21. I refer to the need for an ongoing independent review agency to evaluate government programs and government services, to conduct reliable cost-benefit analysis. I think this is a very valid suggestion and it should be considered. There have been other constructive recommendations advanced. We all have a part to play in this process. We can all offer some reasonable suggestions, and 1 have in mind what my leader said today regarding the restructuring of the committee system with the power of committees to initiate inquiries, or at least examine Crown corporations on a regular basis. It is very fundamental that their annual reports should automatically be referred to the respective committees so the committees can decide whether in fact they will direct a particular Crown corporation to come before them and be held accountable to parliament. Surely that is very basic and elementary.
Most important, the government must not continue to ignore blindly the recommendations of parliament. As my friend, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), pointed out earlier, there have been many occasions in the past six years, I believe there were eight, on which motions emanating from this side of the House were brought forward to deal with the government's mishandling of funds and the loss of parliamentary control. We have raised this matter at various other times during the question period and in the committees, and we have had very little response from the government. The government must, indeed, heed the warnings of the opposition. It must take cognizance of the warning from the public and, indeed, the media, and it must act without delay in implementing the major recommendations of the Auditor General.
I am pleased that the President of the Treasury Board has at least gone part way in fulfilling some of these recommendations. I realize he has a mess to clean up, and he has my sympathy. Hopefully with some time and co-operation he may be able to put the business back on the rails. I am sure he will get support from this side of the House if he responds in a positive and direct fashion.
When we think in terms of financial management and control we must ask ourselves where are we and how did we get here. I think the Auditor General summed it up quite clearly and succinctly with very carefully selected and chosen words. It has been summed up not only in his words but in the words of the combined and collective opinion of a number of professional excutive accountants across the country. The Auditor General said very clearly that the government and, indeed, parliament have lost or are close to losing effective control of the public purse. In other words, he said government spending is out of control. He said the government financial management and control systems are weak, ineffective and, in some cases, grossly inadequate.
Economic Policy
The financial management and control study, which is the study that involved an examination of 28 federal government departments, brought forth very damning evidence contained in last year's report. Our Crown corporations were subject to the same kind of review in the last year, and out of the 27 that were examined there were only two identified as not having some significant weaknesses.
When we look at the Auditor General's report and note some of the alarming revelations there in connection with our Crown corporations, such as the CBC which sends out statements of accounts to its customers only on an annual basis, we can only conclude that if that is the kind of accounting and management practices our Crown corporations are engaged in, they need someone to step on their toes. There is no question about that. In short, the government, its departments, agencies, and now its Crown corporations have financial management and control standards which are significantly below the acceptable standard of quality and effectiveness. There is no question about that.
What brought about this deterioration? As has been pointed out, it did not happen during the term in office of this particular Auditor General. His precedessor did a pretty good job in bringing this matter to the forefront, but many of the former Auditor General's recommendations, as pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River, have yet to be implemented. What is the real reason and what did go wrong?
Quite frankly it is clear that this condition evolved over successive Liberal administrations, particularly since 1968. From that period to the present time we have witnessed a fourfold increase in federal government spending and a huge growth in the amount of money extracted by all levels of government, now approaching 43 per cent of our gross national product. Successive Liberal administrations have deliberately chipped and whittled away at the parliamentary process. They have usurped the job of parliament in the area of financial control, and have effectively destroyed parliament's ability to scrutinize and maintain a watchful eye over financial control. The control mechanisms in respect of the public finances of this country are defunct, to put it mildly. These administrations have done this by streamlining the rules and the estimates, relying upon an ineffective committee structure, and the ineffectiveness has become crystal clear, Mr. Speaker.
The government of the day is no longer held accountable to parliament for its conduct or for the way it spends public money. It seems that the bureaucrats, enough of them to make up a selected elite, have far more power than parliament today under this administration. Government expenditures can no longer be challenged in parliament, they can no longer be properly scrutinized and analysed. There is a built in guillotine rule which leaves the government in a position to simply run out the clock.
When the government is not held accountable to parliament, it is only logical and it follows that the subordinates, the bureaucracy, are not accountable either. This is summed up
