I have a lot of boring material which I insist on putting before the House at this time because I want to deal in very specific terms with the charge that government secrecy deprives hon. members opposite of their role in dealing with fiscal and monetary policy. I want to outline all the opportunities there have been in this session for participation in economic policy making, in fiscal policy making, and in decisions on monetary policy.
No government will give or can give complete disclosure of pending fiscal, economic, and monetary policies. Hon. members cannot expect the government to give, for example, advance notice of the date of the removal of controls, and for the same reason they cannot expect the government to make public the advice it is getting about the appropriate time to remove the controls. That would have an effect on the market, on commercial activities, on jobs and so forth which would be entirely counter productive. They cannot expect to get advance notice of a change in the discount rate of the Bank of Canada, or advice about it. That is not the kind of information which can be made public in advance. They cannot expect to have budgetary changes or possible budgetary changes announced in advance. They cannot expect to have the government put forward its estimated cash requirements for some future period. All these things are the kinds of information which no reasonable person who knows anything about the way an economy operates could expect or consider it desirable to receive in advance. However, that does not deprive the opposition of a genuine role.
In May of this year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) presented in his budget speech to the House a fully documented report on the development of fiscal and monetary policy and on the economic situation and outlook. To assist the debate he tabled in advance the "Economic Review", which provided a comprehensive and factual review of economic developments in Canada, and it was the subject of further discussion in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. When the May 25 budget was presented, it was fully debated in this House, and the co-ordinated thrust of fiscal and monetary policy and of the anti-inflation program was set forth and discussed at length. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) talked about the fact that the government has been warned. We have been warned time and again. I think warnings are an important part of opposition participation in a debate, but I think in a debate on economic

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy
policy when all the facts are on the table, when the "Economic Review" is there, and when the economic outlook is there, more than warnings and threats is called for.
Following an extensive round of consultations during the summer recess the Minister of Finance announced on September 7 a number of modifications to the anti-inflation program. At that time he took the opportunity again to provide a very full accounting of the major progress made in the fight against inflation in the first year of the program, and he also presented a progress report on the operation of fiscal and monetary policy. He referred in particular to the policy of the Bank of Canada and the conduct of monetary operations in relation to monetary supply targets. He provided a further report on the fiscal position, the balance of payments and the developing economic prospects, including the elements of strength and weakness in the short term outlook. Later, in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, the Minister of Finance again reported to the House on the progress of the anti-inflation program, tabling at that time the government's working paper, "The Way Ahead", which provides a framework and an invitation for discussion among all Canadians of the government's longer term view about the evolution and the role of government.
What do we hear from the opposition about "The Way Ahead"? Perhaps some warnings, perhaps some criticism, but what are the proposals of the opposition on the important stress areas in our economy, the areas which require special attention after controls are removed? What would the opposition like us to do? The hon. member for Peace River talked about sunshine and its importance in the government process. If members of the opposition want to propose a new employment strategy in the public sector and in the private sector, that is the kind of proposal which calls for an answer from the government. It puts the government on the spot, but that is not something they have done very often; it is something they have done very rarely.
On October 22 I tabled in the House the first year report of the Anti-Inflation Board, once again detailing publicly and openly the role and operations of the Anti-Inflation Board and the major progress made in reducing inflation in Canada. More recently the Minister of Finance addressed this House during the debate at second reading stage of the income tax bill, Bill C-22. He responded openly to the request from the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) to provide a further updating on the economic situation and outlook, as well as the Fiscal position of the government.
It is also the case that since that time the minister has appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs concerning supplementary estimates (B) and presented himself for a broad range of questioning on economic affairs.
This is a long list and I could make it longer, Mr. Speaker, but as you can see, on all these occasions since last May, the government has provided a full and frank accounting of economic policy and the state of the economy. This approach by

the government can hardly be characterized as secrecy or non-disclosure. There was particular reference to the secrecy of economic studies and projections but it ought to be understood that the process of economic analysis and forecasting is a continually evolving one. New information becomes available, external developments occur, data is revised and updated. The process is fraught with uncertainty. In the last analysis the Minister of Finance must make his own judgments and report to the House as carefully and as confidently as he can on the situation and prospects. This he has done time and again.
There have been comments and, I believe, misunderstandings on the part of the opposition about the role of the Department of Finance in relation to the forecasts of the OECD. I should like to set the record straight again on that score for the benefit of hon. members, recognizing that this matter was looked at in the standing committee.
From time to time, both members of this House and economic commentators have raised the question as to the nature of communications between officials of the Department of Finance and OECD officials during the period of time leading up to the publication by the OECD of their semi-annual assessment of short term economic prospects. I would therefore like to outline briefly what in fact is the nature of the communications between the two organizations and, by so doing, underline the fact that the views expressed by the OECD in their report are their own. The published forecasts for member nations can easily be, and often are, at variance with the views held by officials of the member countries.
Each June and December, the OECD publishes a document titled "The Economic Outlook" which contains short run macro-economic projections for the economies of the OECD member countries. In addition, a brief commentary on recent economic conditions and policies is provided for the OECD countries as a group and for the larger countries on an individual basis. The forecasts appearing in this document are prepared by, and are therefore the responsibility of, the OECD. There are, however, both advantages and disadvantages faced by the OECD in the preparation of this material. Their geographic and physical remoteness from the country under study is an advantage because of taking an objective view; in a sense it is also a disadvantage because certain information can only be received second hand and the data may age rapidly.
It is in recognition of these shortcomings that the OECD secretariat convenes a series of meetings of officials of all of the member countries in the weeks prior to the publication of its Outlook document. At these meetings, officials of each country have the opportunity to comment on various aspects of the preliminary forecasts that have been prepared by the OECD secretariat for their country or any other country. The OECD benefits from this exchange in that they receive updates as to recent trends in economic data, as well as the professional analytic views of their colleagues in the member countries. Officials in the member countries benefit by being able to probe officials directly of both the OECD and other member countries as to economic conditions and prospects in
December 9, 1976

the OECD as a whole and in individual countries. Given the high degree of interdependence of the economies of the OECD countries, this type of exchange of course plays a vital role in the co-ordination of economic policy among countries.
Subsequent to these meetings, the OECD finalize the view that will be published in the Outlook. Of course, this final view will have had the benefit of the working level exchange between professional staff of the OECD secretariat and of the member nations. But it must be emphasized that the final decisions and responsibility for the forecasts rest solely with the OECD; the forecast may or may not be in accord with the views held by member countries.
It should also be noted-and this is something that is forgotten time and time again in the warnings offered to us by the opposition-that the OECD makes use of a methodological approach often employed in preparing short term economic forecasts. It is assumed that current policies in member countries are retained in an unchanged way over the forecast period. In addition, exchange rate changes are not forecast. Thus any policy or exchange rate changes that occur subsequent to the preparation of these forecasts means that the projections must be amended to reflect these changes.
I remember when an article appeared in the Wall Street Journal which was the subject of questions from the opposition, it was suggested that the OECD forecasts were not only prepared by the government or known to the government- which was not the case-but that they were absolutely valid. What was also not recognized in the question put to us was that just in the few days preceding, an important employment policy strategy had been announced by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), and there had been a reduction in the discount rate of the Bank of Canada. All these factors had to be taken into consideration.
I think I can conclude a little ahead of my time, Mr. Speaker, by noting that the opposition has great opportunities, it has all kinds of information but-it has blown it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the member who has just taken his seat has read a good deal of meaningless trivia, the sole purpose of which seems to have been to take up time and prevent members of the opposition from taking part in this debate.
Hear, hear!

I rise for the purpose of supporting the motion which condemns the government for its inept handling of public finances. I wish to address myself particularly to the amendment moved by the national leader of this party, which condemns the government for its failure to establish mechanisms to achieve effective supervisory financial control over Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and other Crown corporations.
It is rather significant that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) who spoke this afternoon, and the other
Economic Policy
government speakers who have participated in this debate, carefully stayed away from the whole question of financial control over Crown corporations.
The Auditor General said that the government was in danger of losing control of its finances but, Mr. Speaker, in the case of Crown corporations it lost control of the finances of those organizations long ago. Anyone who has sat in this House for the last ten or 12 years knows that most of the Crown corporations have never been examined by a committee of the House and that there are no regular reports to the committees of the House, no assessment of policy, no examination of expenditures-there is virtually no control.
One of the things that ought to be done in this parliament is that the reports and financial statements of Crown corporations should be referred to the appropriate standing committee, or by statute form a special committee of this parliament with authority to sit whether the House is sitting or not, to examine the financial statements of all Crown corporations. These Crown corporations are spending billions of dollars of the people's money and there is no adequate control or accountability either with respect to expenditures or with respect to the policies they follow.
The hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) asked the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) whether he thought Crown corporations should be controlled by the government. To ask the question is surely to answer it, Mr. Speaker. Nobody thinks that the government should have day to day control. After all, what is a Crown corporation? A Crown corporation is set up by the government under the authority of parliament to carry on certain business transactions on behalf of the people of Canada. It is responsible to parliament through a minister of the Crown and therefore, surely, both the government and this House have some right to hold it accountable with respect to the money it is spending, which belongs to the people of Canada, and with respect to whether it is serving the best interests of the people of Canada. Neither of these things is being done today by the Crown corporations, and no Liberal member who took part in the debate, including the President of the Treasury Board, even touched on this question. If you need an illustration of what I mean look at the three instances which have been brought to the attention of the people of Canada in the last few weeks by the present Auditor General and the previous one.
Let us consider the case of AECL. It has been referred to, but I want to document it. AECL negotiated a contract to sell a CANDU reactor to South Korea. On December 30, 1974, the president of AECL confirmed by letter that an agreement was being negotiated to pay an agent, Mr. Shaul Eisenberg of Tel Aviv, the sum of $17 million, plus $3 million at the rate of $500,000 a year. In the first place I do not know why you would need an agent. The Government of Canada was going to sell a reactor to the government of South Korea.

That was in conformity with this government's humanitarian tendencies.

December 9, 1976
Economic Policy

In any
event, they thought they needed an agent and they were going to pay him $20 million. The contract was signed on January 27, 1975, and came into force on January 26, 1976. However, a new president of AECL had been appointed. He took the matter up with the minister and with the chairman of the board, so that the minister has known about this for many months. The agreement was renegotiated. And what did that renegotiation amount to? It amounted to the sum of $15,373,181. That was made up of $5,142,393, or 1 per cent of the commission, because the reactor cost $514 million; expenses of $8,098,500, to which I will come in a few moments; interest for delay of payment of invoices of $132,289, and advance payment for post-contract services of $2 million, with the commitment to pay $175,000 every quarter, or $700,000 a year during the period of the agreement. That was simply an advance payment of $2 million.
The interesting things to look at are the expenses, because there were expenses of more than $8 million for which no particulars were available. According to the details, payments were made to consultants. Whom did they turn out to be? They turned out to be Industrial Export of Frankfurt, Germany, and International Shipping and Building Establishment in Hong Kong, both of which were owned by Mr. Shaul Eisenberg, located in the same office and using the same telephone; so that by renegotiating the agreement Mr. Eisenberg made virtually the same amount of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The government was helping the Third World.

The $15
million which the corporation agreed to pay is in addition to a provision for the payment of $700,000 a year for the rest of the agreement. Since the previous agreement provided for the payment for six years, for the life of the contract, if you multiply six by $700,000 and add that sum to the other sum mentioned, you will see that approximately $18.5 million will be paid to Mr. Eisenberg. Mr. Speaker, $18.5 million is not a great deal less than $20 million.
The interesting thing is that not only was a good amount of these expenses paid to the other dummy companies set up by Mr. Eisenberg, but $5,400,000 was spent for which the only explanation on the invoice was the written notation that the expenditures were allocated in accordance with the agent's instructions. Now, no auditor would pass that under ordinary circumstances. No self-respecting company would expect to get away with a statement like that; yet here was a situation in which the taxpayers' money was frittered away, paid out-the ultimate sum will be close to $20 million-to an agent whose services have not yet been defined. Five point four million dollars was paid out without any explanation at all.
The other deal with which hon. members are familiar has to do with the CANDU reactor sale in Argentina. In that case on April 19, 1974, the president of AECL authorized the payment of $2,415 million to an unnamed commercial agent for services rendered during negotiations for the sale of a reactor
(Mr. Stanfield.]
to Argentina. In that case we did not even pay the money to an agent. The deal was negotiated by Italimpianti, which billed AECL $2,415 million. As the Auditor General said, these invoices were not supported by an agreement or invoice from the agent. Actually the money was paid, as hon. members know, into a bank in Liechtenstein, to the account of Intercontinental Trading Establishment. Significantly, we have been trying all week to discover to whom this money was paid. The minister admitted he did not know, but he is trying to find out. And how has he done that? He has been making inquiries of Italimpianti in Italy. Surely if you, Sir, were trying to find out why money was paid, you would at least get on the telephone. If you could not get results that way, you would put your ablest accountant on a flight, and send him over to Italy-
What, with taxpayers' money?

-to ask
those people what they did.
The taxpayers' money would be paying for that trip.
Oh, oh!
Is the minister concerned about taxpayers' money?

There you have it; it would be wasting the taxpayers' money if the government made an effort to find out what the government did with $2.4 million. Talk about being penny wise and pound foolish! That is exactly the kind of thinking which is prevalent in this government.
The hon. lady became a cabinet minister awfully fast.
Talk to Otto Lang.
That is typical of this government's humanitarianism to the Third World.

The other marvellous piece of business which was conducted had to do with the situation brought to the attention of the government by the former Auditor General, Mr. Maxwell Henderson, who wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) calling his attention to two matters. First, he pointed out that a good deal of machination had been going on with regard to the Polymer Corporation. What has come out of it? The government has done nothing. The Prime Minister asked for an investigation. Nothing was done.
There was a telephone call by one of the ministers. Anthony Hampson, who was president of the CDC, said he would certainly suspect that they were minimizing taxes, but they were not a taxing authority.
December 9, 1976

Mr. Ian Rush, the President of Polysar, said his firm gave cash rebates to international customers for volume purchases. However, that does not explain why the rebates were placed in numbered accounts.
Surely that is not a satisfactory way in which to run the affairs of this country. The time has come when the government ought to be held responsible for the actions it has taken. 1 urge the government to come clean with the people of this country and tell them what has been going on.
It is perfectly apparent that in these transactions public funds have been squandered. They have been used very improperly, and we have had no satisfactory explanation from the government. The people of Canada want a much more satisfactory explanation than we have had to date with reference to this whole deal. They want an accounting, and they want it fast. We are going to get it eventually. It is not going to die. The members of this House and the people of this country will insist that the government give a much more satisfactory explanation. That explanation will not be found in the Public Accounts Committee, where it is being smothered. It will be found by a royal commission looking into this matter, getting the facts out into the daylight.
Hear, hear!
